矩阵与归约流水：布局、资源和完成依赖\\\\n\\\\n一个 GPU kernel 的设计同时决定数据怎样进入计算单元、哪个线程持有什么片段、临时状态占多少资源，以及何时允许覆盖。tile 更大、流水更深或矩阵指令更多，都只有在这些关系成立时才可能改善性能。\\\\n\\\\n## GEMM 的数据依赖与资源账\\\\n\\\\n对 C=A·B，令输出块为 Mₜ×Nₜ、沿归约轴每次处理 Kₜ。一个阶段读取 A 的 Mₜ×Kₜ 片段和 B 的 Kₜ×Nₜ 片段，输出 accumulator 跨多个 K 阶段保留。数据依赖是：全局读取 → 片上数据就绪 → 矩阵乘加 → accumulator 可消费 → epilogue → 输出可见。下一个 K 阶段的读取可以提前，但不能覆盖仍被矩阵指令读取的片上缓冲。\\\\n\\\\n若输入每元素 s 字节、流水深度 n，单 block 的输入缓冲主项为 n·s·(MₜKₜ+KₜNₜ)，输出累加主项为 a·MₜNₜ，a 为累加元素字节。还要计入对齐、barrier、转置区、地址与 epilogue 临时量。共享存储、寄存器、线程数和 block 数约束共同限制驻留；仅检查共享存储够用不足以证明没有 spill。\\\\n\\\\n设定 Mₜ=Nₜ=128、Kₜ=64、输入 2 字节、累加 4 字节。每级输入缓冲为 32 KiB，三级为 96 KiB；输出 accumulator 为 64 KiB。若由 128 个线程均摊，仅输出就平均需要每线程 128 个 32 bit 寄存器，尚未计其他变量。改成两级减少 32 KiB 片上缓冲，但能否增加驻留 block，还取决于寄存器与目标架构限制。这个算例描述资源占用，不指定任意 GPU 的最佳 tile。\\\\n\\\\n## 先适配指令布局，再安排线程\\\\n\\\\n矩阵指令要求的 fragment 布局不等于用户矩阵的行列布局。全局合并访问、共享存储 bank、矩阵操作数布局与输出写回应作为一条路径比较。局部转置或 swizzle 增加地址/搬运工作，却可能减少非合并事务和 bank 冲突；也可能让后续消费者再支付一次转换。\\\\n\\\\n固定来源中，[FlashAttention-3 v1](../sources/S-FLASHATTENTION3.md) §2–3 以 Hopper 的 TMA、异步 WGMMA 和 warpgroup 组织流水，warpgroup 由 4 个 warp 组成。这是具体架构上的实现入口。[ROCm 固定文档](../sources/S-ROCM.md) 则描述 CDNA 的 MFMA、VGPR/AGPR 与 LDS。两条路径的线程片段、寄存器资源和异步能力需要分别核实，不能将 CUDA 指令、32 线程约定或某一 bank 数直接替换成 AMD 名称。\\\\n\\\\n相同 dtype 也可能有不同操作数布局限制。FA3 对 FP8 的讨论说明，前一 GEMM 的 accumulator 要交给后一 GEMM 时，转换与排列是实际成本；FP16 路径可用不意味着只更改 dtype 就能得到合法 FP8 kernel。低精度还要重新验证 scale、累加、异常值和任务质量。\\\\n\\\\n## 一个完整的非矩阵指令映射：两 warp 共享输入\\\\n\\\\n先把逻辑算法落实到可检查的普通线程运算，再考虑改用矩阵指令。定义 A∈ℝᴹˣᴷ、B∈ℝᴷˣᴺ，均按行连续保存，输出 C∈ℝᴹˣᴺ；本例只计算 C=AB，不读取旧 C，没有 bias 或其他 epilogue。输入和输出为 FP32，累加也为 FP32；数学参考使用实数求和，真实运算是否融合乘加及其舍入另行核验。维度可为零，K=0 时有效输出为零，M=0 或 N=0 时不启动输出工作。\\\\n\\\\n选择一个 CTA 的输出 tile 为16×32，归约阶段为8，CTA有64线程。输出块坐标为 (m₀,n₀)=(16bₘ,32bₙ)，阶段 j 的归约起点 k₀=8j，共 J=⌈K/8⌉ 阶段。这个小例子旨在展示映射与生命周期，没有声称它能接近矩阵单元吞吐。\\\\n\\\\n线程编号 τ=32w+λ，其中 w∈{0,1} 是 warp，λ∈[0,31] 是 lane。warp w 独占本输出块第16w至16w+15列。lane λ 保存8个累加量，令 u∈[0,7]，i=λ+32u，则它负责局部坐标 r=⌊i/16⌋=2u+⌊λ/16⌋、c=16w+(i mod16)。64×8=512个坐标恰好覆盖16×32输出，没有重复写者，也不需要跨 warp 合并输出。\\\\n\\\\n每个输入槽保存行主序共享矩阵 Aˢ[16,8] 和 Bˢ[8,32]。全体64线程按线性下标搬运：Aˢ 的 a=τ+64v，v=0,1，映射为 (⌊a/8⌋,a mod8)；Bˢ 的 b=τ+64v，v=0,1,2,3，映射为 (⌊b/32⌋,b mod32)。每个共享位置有唯一写者。若全局基址是 pA、pB、pC，字节地址为：\\\\n\\\\n- A：pA+4[(m₀+r)K+(8j+k)]，前提 m₀+r<M 且8j+k<K。\\\\n- B：pB+4[(8j+k)N+(n₀+c)]，前提8j+k<K 且 n₀+c<N。\\\\n- C：pC+4[(m₀+r)N+(n₀+c)]，前提 m₀+r<M 且 n₀+c<N。\\\\n\\\\n非法输入位置填零，且不计算、解引用越界地址；非法输出位置不写回，但其线程仍参加规定的集体同步。对 K 尾块，A/B 的同一无效归约项都为零，因此补齐到8不改变有效 C。全局地址按各自实际 stride 计算，共享地址按本节定义的紧密布局计算，不能把两者混用。\\\\n\\\\n设 M=19、N=35、K=17，选最后输出块 m₀=16、n₀=32。j=1、局部 r=2、k=3、c=2 对应 A[18,11]、B[11,34]、C[18,34]，相对基址字节偏移分别为1268、1676、2656。j=2只有归约位置16有效；这个输出块只有3×3个合法输出。此处行跨度68/140字节，不具有统一的16字节行对齐；4字节元素复制合法，不能给整行虚构更强的对齐证明。\\\\n\\\\n消费者按 k=0…7 读 Aˢ[r,k] 与 Bˢ[k,c]，更新自己持有的8个累加量。两个 warp 共享 A，分别读取 B 的不同16列。以固定 u、k 的标量共享读取为例，同一 warp 的两组16 lane各读同一 A 值；B读取16个不同字，每字被两 lane读取。依据[共享存储广播与 bank 规则](../sources/S-CUDA-BEST.md)，相同字的多 lane读取是广播，不能按32次独立事务计费；若改变行跨度或lane坐标，需要重算实际冲突。协作写共享时，字下标 τ+64v 的 bank 为 λ，单条标量写指令覆盖32个不同 bank。\\\\n\\\\n这条路径已连续给出逻辑 tile、元素地址、线程归属、共享布局和输出写回。把标量 k 循环换成矩阵指令时，仍要另外证明形状、dtype、布局、参与线程和完成依赖；并非保持这份 lane 所有权就能直接替换指令。[Attention 的 warp 矩阵实例](../frameworks/attention-backends.md)采用公开的矩阵装载/存储接口交接，明确不假定内部 fragment 的 lane/寄存器排列。跨指令或平台应重新核对契约。\\\\n\\\\n## 从一个槽到多槽：每代数据的完整协议\\\\n\\\\n定义 d≥1 个槽，每槽的身份为 (s,g,j)，s=j mod d、g=⌊j/d⌋。一个槽从“空闲”到“复制中”，再到“可读”，最后到“读者全部结束”。槽内的 A/B 有同一个逻辑阶段 j，但可以由多条复制组成；仅完成 A 或某一线程发出的复制，不足以宣布整个槽可读。两个 warp 都是 A 的读者，各自又是对应 B 半块的读者；本例保守地将整个 A/B 槽一起释放。\\\\n\\\\n这里区分三类完成：复制完成使相应字节到达共享存储；具有正确作用域的同步使消费者能安全观察这些写入；每个消费者完成最后一次共享读取，才允许下一代覆盖。消费者若改成异步矩阵指令，线程发射返回也不等于指令结束读取；必须以该指令规定的完成条件释放。不同槽的复制可以提前，某槽的代次不能提前。\\\\n\\\\n下面是本例的一种完整组织。复制过程可由硬件异步操作承担，也可由同步加载实现；伪代码中的“等待”明确表达依赖，不指定某个 CUDA API 的机械一一替换。若把两个 warp 的完成合并为 CTA barrier，所有64线程都必须以一致顺序到达。\\\\n\\\\n```pseudocode\\\\n输入：A、B、M/N/K、输出块坐标、d≥1\\\\n所有lane的8个累加量初始化为0；建立d个空闲槽及各代次\\\\n定义提交阶段(j)：\\\\n    s←j mod d，g←floor(j/d)\\\\n    确认槽s上一代全部复制/写者及两个warp读者已结束\\\\n    设置本代身份(s,g,j)，清除本代完成状态\\\\n    全体线程按上述地址划分：合法元素复制，无效元素写零\\\\n    将本代所有输入写入纳入同一个完成契约；提交复制票据\\\\n若J=0：只写有效输出零，结束\\\\n启动：依次提交 j=0…min(d,J)−1\\\\n对j=0…J−1：\\\\n    等待身份(s,g,j)的全部复制与零填完成，并建立CTA可见性\\\\n    每个warp按k=0…7消费A/B，更新它独占的输出累加量\\\\n    每个warp在最后共享读取完成后到达本代“读完”条件\\\\n    等待两个warp都读完；此后槽s才可释放\\\\n    若j+d<J：提交阶段(j+d)，把新复制与后续已就绪阶段的计算重叠\\\\n排空：确认全部已提交票据和消费者结束，不产生未消费阶段\\\\n每个lane只向有效(m₀+r,n₀+c)写自己的8个结果\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nJ=1时只提交和消费阶段0；J=2时只消费0、1，不访问并不存在的“下一块”；J=0时不等待未创建的票据。d大于J时多出的槽为空闲，静态分配仍可能为它们付容量。每个阶段被消费恰好一次，输出在处理前 j 个阶段后等于这 j 段乘积之和；同一输出的累加次序始终沿 j、k递增，warp的不同调度顺序不改变其拥有的输出集合。\\\\n\\\\n取消也不能跳过已参与的集体同步，或让一部分线程提前退出。可以在统一边界停止提交新阶段，排空已提交复制和消费者，再放弃输出；若必须保留部分结果，则另外定义它对应哪些归约区间。本章的 C=AB 没有将部分 C 发布为完整结果的语义。\\\\n\\\\n本例采用“整个输入槽等两个warp”的保守释放。若仅等第一个warp、或只等复制票据结束，就可能在第二warp仍读取旧 A 时写入新阶段。若精细拆开A/B资源，A必须等两个warp，B各半块可以分别等对应warp；那需要独立身份和复用条件。减少等待的收益要与增加的同步状态比较，不是多计几个barrier就自动更可靠。\\\\n\\\\n## 抽象票据怎样落实到 CUDA 的同步契约\\\\n\\\\n固定 [CUDA 12.8 指南](../sources/S-CUDA-ASYNC.md) §7.26–7.28区分了 barrier阶段、异步复制与多级pipeline。普通线程的共享写入可通过CTA同步建立可见性，但单独的CTA同步不能替代尚未完成的异步复制等待。反过来，一个线程等完自身复制，也不能自动证明其他线程的复制已完成或所有读者已结束。必须核对同步对象的参与者和作用域，保证全部生产者写入被消费者等待所覆盖。\\\\n\\\\n指南所述 global→shared 硬件异步复制可采用4/8/16字节粒度，要求对应大小与地址对齐；API还可能做运行时检查或采用其他实现。128字节对齐是其性能建议，不是任意合法4字节复制必须满足的数学条件。本例的尾部可采用受保护的4字节复制与普通零填；将两类写入一起纳入CTA可见性，禁止为越界向量读伪造对齐或有效字节证明。\\\\n\\\\ncommit/arrive 等操作的参与线程应保持约定的收敛执行。固定文档描述 warp 内实际批次序列与各线程感知序列可能因分歧而不同，造成额外等待；把“每线程循环次数相同”当成完整证明不够。barrier初始化要先于参与者使用，每一代的预期到达与真实参与者一致；退出需遵循其协议。本章的无效输出lane继续参与，正是为保留这一集体契约。\\\\n\\\\n若硬件没有相应异步加速，普通加载、寄存器中转与共享写入也能实现相同数学算法和槽生命周期，但会多付指令、寄存器和可能暴露的等待。异步API被接受、生成了异步指令、实际发生有益重叠，是三种不同结论。\\\\n\\\\n## 工作、交通、同步与驻留必须使用同一候选\\\\n\\\\n本例一个完整归约阶段做2×16×32×8=8192 FLOPs，读取512字节A和1024字节B，共1536字节有效输入请求；一个完整输出块最终写2048字节。对所有输出tile，令 Gₘ=⌈M/16⌉、Gₙ=⌈N/32⌉。若每个CTA独立读取它需要的输入且尾部不越界，A请求约为4MKGₙ，B请求约为4KNGₘ，输出为4MN；输入的唯一持久字节则只有4(MK+KN)。前者体现CTA之间重读，后者体现数据驻留，二者都不是已测的设备主存事务。\\\\n\\\\npadding可能使计算仍执行2×16×32×8×GₘGₙJ FLOPs，而有效函数工作是2MKN；M/N/K很小时无效lane和尾部工作不能忽略。按每个乘加各读取两个共享标量计，一个完整阶段的消费者逻辑共享读取为32768字节，另有1536字节生产者共享写入。广播与cache改变物理交通；这些逻辑字节不能再次除设备主存带宽加入总时间。共享读者通信没有网络通信，跨CTA拆分归约才另外引入部分结果写读及合并边界。\\\\n\\\\n每槽输入容量1536字节，d槽为1536d字节；本例64线程×8个FP32累加量为2048字节逻辑状态，每线程8个32bit累加量。实际寄存器还含地址、循环、暂存、编译器分配及任何中转，不能用2048字节直接宣称真实寄存器占用。barrier、对齐、调试区或epilogue另计。旧的大tile算例同样成立：128×128×64、FP16输入每级32KiB，3级96KiB，FP32输出逻辑累加64KiB；128线程均摊仅累加就相当于每线程128个32bit值。\\\\n\\\\n设每CTA共享分配 S(d)、实际分配寄存器 R(d)、线程数 T，目标SM相应容量为 Sₛₘ、Rₛₘ、Tₛₘ，warp上限 Wₛₘ、block上限 Bₛₘ。忽略分配粒度时，同时驻留CTA数至多为 min(⌊Sₛₘ/S(d)⌋,⌊Rₛₘ/R(d)⌋,⌊Tₛₘ/T⌋,⌊Wₛₘ/⌈T/32⌉⌋,Bₛₘ)。真实配置还受每block上限和资源分配粒度约束，应按编译结果与目标机核对。减线程数可能增加每线程累加和寄存器需求，不能从线程项变松直接推出驻留上升。\\\\n\\\\n完整调用还包括参数/描述符准备、可能的编译与布局转换、launch、kernel首尾和输出交接。准备若被多次调用复用，以真正复用次数摊销；转换若每次发生，以每次计费。copy等待已在kernel关键路径里，就不能作为额外同步再次加上。深流水没有消除等待，而是让部分等待被独立计算覆盖；暴露多少取决于资源和输入规模。\\\\n\\\\n## 延迟模型、首尾与一个选择反转\\\\n\\\\n只用每块加载时间L与计算时间C写 max(L,C)，会混淆复制延迟与复制吞吐。定义 L为发出一阶段后数据就绪的延迟，I为复制通路允许相邻阶段发出的最小间隔，C为消费者处理一阶段的时间。以下理想模型假设复制可流水、各阶段顺序消费、同一个CTA串行消费、槽直到消费结束才复用；发出成本已包括在I内，无额外干预。令 xⱼ为发出时间、yⱼ为消费完成时间：\\\\n\\\\n```pseudocode\\\\nx₀←0，y₋₁←0\\\\n对阶段j依次计算：\\\\n    若j>0：xⱼ←xⱼ₋₁+I\\\\n    若j≥d：xⱼ←max(xⱼ,yⱼ₋d)       # 旧读者结束才有槽\\\\n    yⱼ←max(xⱼ+L,yⱼ₋₁)+C\\\\nJ=0时kernel内部阶段耗时为0，否则取最后阶段的y\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n此递推是理想设备可以及时发出复制的乐观时序；普通“全CTA只在消费完成后提交新槽”的上节伪代码不一定实现它的所有发出时刻。例如空闲槽很多时，其预取提交在启动段已发生；稳态若需要计算中途更及时发出，可采用专门生产者或更合适的指令调度，仍要保持同一完成协议。不能把理想下界直接称为所写伪代码的真实耗时。\\\\n\\\\n长序列稳态平均周期受到 I、C、(L+C)/d 三项下界限制；后者来自每个槽从发出到消费结束至少占用L+C时间。有限J必须使用递推或实际时间线，首块始终先付L再付C，不能用 J·max(I,C)抹去首尾。d达到足够覆盖后继续增加没有必然吞吐收益。\\\\n\\\\n全部为设定值：L=6、I=2、C=3，单位记为τ。J=8时，d=1的完成时刻为9、18、…、72；d=2为9、12、18、21、27、30、36、39；d=3为9、12、15、18、21、24、27、30。单CTA三级39→30τ有收益，四级仍为30τ。J=1各候选均为9τ；J=2时d=1为18τ，d≥2的候选为12τ，第三槽没有收益。这里没有从阶段数推断GPU的真实L/I/C。\\\\n\\\\n再设一个用于隔离容量影响的假想SM：扣除固定状态后只剩6KiB用于这些输入槽，其他block/线程/寄存器限制允许至少两个CTA；同步对象另外预留且不占这6KiB。两级每CTA3072字节，允许两CTA，三级4608字节只允许一CTA。若在各自驻留下每CTA服务时间仍分别为39和30τ、无共享通路额外争用，4个CTA的保守分波估计为两级2×39=78τ、三级4×30=120τ。单CTA胜者反而输掉整网格。这个6KiB不是某真实GPU规格；共享复制通路或带宽争用存在时，L/I/C必须作为驻留数的函数重测，不能独立复制单CTA曲线。\\\\n\\\\n如果有效共享预算提高至9KiB，三级可同时容纳两个CTA，同一假设下4CTA变成60τ，优于两级78τ；若J=1，多一个槽依旧不加速。改变工作网格、每CTA寄存器、K长度或复制吞吐，都能改变选择。还可能通过不同tile或精细释放B半块改变模型；保留哪个候选由合法域、资源和校准后的关键路径决定。\\\\n\\\\n## Attention 中归约与矩阵流水怎样连接\\\\n\\\\nQ tile 与多块 K/V 组合时，QK 产生分数，在线 softmax 更新每行最大值 m 和归一化质量 ℓ，随后把加权 V 合入未归一化输出 U。若最大值从 mₒ 改为 mₙ，旧质量与旧 U 都要乘 exp(mₒ−mₙ)，最后才用 ℓ 归一化；完整推导见 [attention IO](../algorithms/attention-io.md)。\\\\n\\\\n核对缩放方向的设定反例：两块分数分别为 0、2，对应 V 分别为 1、0。输出应为 1/(1+exp(2))≈0.1192，落在 V 的凸包内。若把旧累加量向相反方向放大，会立即破坏该关系。应从归一化恒等式检查伪代码，不能仅因材料是固定论文就照抄所有公式排版。\\\\n\\\\nQK、softmax、PV 在同一块内有顺序依赖；跨块或跨 warpgroup 可以重叠部分矩阵与标量工作，但要同时保留所需分数、概率和输出代次。额外 Bq×Bk 分数片段会增加寄存器压力。增大 Bq 提高 K/V 重用，增大 Bk 改变加载和归约粒度；长历史 decode 的少量 query 又可能需要拆分 KV 以获得并行度，再支付部分统计合并成本。\\\\n\\\\n## 如何验证选择及其反转\\\\n\\\\n在代表 shape 上分别比较单/多级缓冲、普通/专门分工、不同 tile 和融合程度。检查实际生成的指令路径、共享存储与寄存器、spill、内存事务及时间线，而不把源代码中的异步调用当成已经重叠的证据。正确性覆盖非整除尾部、全 mask 行、不同历史长度、GQA 映射和归约次序。\\\\n\\\\n短输入或小矩阵可能由启动与调度支配，深流水的启动/收尾反而较贵；长 prefill 更容易摊薄这些成本；长历史小 batch decode 可能受 KV 带宽与并行度约束。最终对照还要回到服务 SLO，避免局部 kernel 的工作区或驻留资源挤占可服务请求。\\\\n\\\\n## 诊断案例：三级为何比两级慢\\\\n\\\\n设已经确认两候选产生相同容许误差的输出，输入、tile、线程映射、计时边界与预热条件相同，仅改变缓冲级数。在目标机测得三级更慢，至少要区分下表的竞争解释。下表是待实施的实验推理，不是本库已经测得的GPU结果。\\\\n\\\\n| 解释 | 可区分的预测 | 保持可比的干预与观测 | 什么结果要求修正解释 |\\\\n|---|---|---|---|\\\\n| 首尾比重增加 | 长K时固定额外代价被摊薄，稳态斜率应更好或接近；J很小时差距大 | 固定tile与实现，扫J，拟合固定项和每阶段项；逐次计时而非只计峰值吞吐 | 三级的长J斜率更坏，不能再只归因首尾 |\\\\n| 寄存器压力造成spill | 三级新增local读写，寄存器/片段生存区间改变，长J也持续支付交通 | 检查实际生成程序和local交通；缩小非关键临时量或改变其生存区间，再以相同计算验证 | 未出现spill或消除spill后仍不改善，需要其他解释；“寄存器数高”本身不等于spill |\\\\n| 驻留降低 | 单CTA三级可能更快，足够CTA的整网格反而慢；共享/寄存器限制对应驻留台阶 | 分开比较单CTA与多CTA，记录实际资源和活跃CTA；只改变可用资源或tile时重新记录工作量 | 驻留不变且未受资源限制时，这个解释缺少支持 |\\\\n| 没有形成预期重叠 | 源程序增加异步表达，实际复制/矩阵指令或等待位置却未改善，暴露空洞仍在 | 查生成指令与依赖，使用时间线/受限微实验；保持工作量检查copy与compute是否能独立推进 | 等待确实减少但运行变慢，应调查新增交通/驻留，不能仍称“没有重叠” |\\\\n| 准备或转换增加 | 只看kernel可能改善，完整调用却变慢；重复复用准备后差距应改变 | 分别记录准备、转换、kernel和输出可消费时刻，按真实复用频率比较 | 差距全在kernel内时，准备不能解释它 |\\\\n\\\\n给一个可复算的反驳过程。若两级时间模型为T₂=10+2J，三级为T₃=18+1.7J，单位均τ，则J=8时26对31.6、J=64时138对126.8，交点约26.67。“小输入三级慢主要因为首尾”与这组设定一致。随后若新增长输入观测却符合T₃′=18+2.4J，J=64时为171.6，则更大的固定项已经不足以解释，必须调查稳态瓶颈。所有值为合成观测，不能放入运行观测库冒充设备测量。\\\\n\\\\n若再发现三级共享分配超过某个驻留台阶、local交通没有增加，应把“spill导致更慢”的假设降级，优先检验资源驻留；但驻留和未重叠可以同时发生，消除一个因素后仍需复测完整边界。只降低寄存器上限可能诱发更多spill，不是隔离驻留的干净实验。改变tile也同时改变复用、任务数和算术强度，应明确这些混杂，而非把每次变快都归因于唯一指标。差异落在重复测量的不确定区间时保留未知，方法见[统计实验](../tools/statistical-experiments.md)。\\\\n\\\\n正确性诊断使用与性能假设分开的反例：K=0/1/7/8/9/17，M/N非整除，交换两warp结束次序，延迟最后一次复制；用独立稠密参考检查每个输出，再注入“只等一个读者”“把旧代票据当新代”“少消费最后阶段”“将全局stride误用为共享stride”。先确认这些错误确实可被检查发现，才讨论流水更快。标量参考与有限事件模型不能证明真实GPU的作用域、可见性或内存竞态均正确。\\\\n\\\\n## 流水的首尾与短输入必须单独推导\\\\n\\\\n固定 [FA3 v1](../sources/S-FLASHATTENTION3.md) 的多级伪代码展示了重叠意图，但打印的循环边界和部分状态交接不足以直接作为实现。例如两阶段示意在只有两块 K/V 时，需要明确计算第二块分数，并依次使用两块各自的概率与 V；不能让循环为空后仍引用未生成的最后概率。独立时序表应保证每个必要 K/V 块恰好计算一次、输出使用同一最大值尺度、收尾按最终归一化分母处理，并覆盖 1、2、3 块、非整除尾部和取消前的最后访问。\\\\n\\\\n其三阶段实验也说明，更多理论重叠可能因额外概率片段和缩放状态挤占寄存器，迫使 tile 变小；实际编译结果又未得到预期的全部重叠。因此候选选择应同时比较算法依赖、生成指令和资源占用，不能只比较源代码里的阶段数。\\\\n\\\\n## 没有 TMA 与线程块簇时的流水组织\\\\n\\\\n固定 CUDA 12.8.0 编程指南的特性表将TMA单元、线程块簇与分布式共享存储支持的边界列为CC 9.0，将所述global→shared硬件加速异步复制与硬件split arrive/wait barrier的边界列为CC 8.0。这里说的是所列特性的硬件支持，不能由没有硬件加速推出不存在软件同步。本章的生产者/消费者与复用依赖也不要求某一代专有指令。\\\\n\\\\n同为8.x也不能共用一组容量。固定指南Table 24列出下列值；其中KB按1024字节解释。它们是规格上限，不保证编译出的kernel达到该驻留，较大动态共享分配还需满足相应配置与opt-in条件。\\\\n\\\\n| CC | 每SM线程/warp上限 | 每SM共享上限 | 每block共享上限 |\\\\n|---|---:|---:|---:|\\\\n| 8.0 | 2048 / 64 | 164KiB | 163KiB |\\\\n| 8.6 | 1536 / 48 | 100KiB | 99KiB |\\\\n| 8.7 | 1536 / 48 | 164KiB | 163KiB |\\\\n| 8.9 | 1536 / 48 | 100KiB | 99KiB |\\\\n| 9.0 | 2048 / 64 | 228KiB | 227KiB |\\\\n\\\\n全局到共享存储的加载：没有TMA时，可以由线程计算地址，通过普通加载或可用的异步复制指令搬运。对齐、swizzle和索引可能增加发射与寄存器需求。cp.async可使用4/8/16字节片段，按所用接口的批次/同步对象等候；TMA处理多维描述符与事务完成时有不同契约。一次tile复制不等于物理上只有一笔事务，任何路径都应区分描述符数、发出指令与实际存储事务。\\\\n\\\\n跨block的部分和交换：选择不同CTA各算一段归约时，常规独立CTA实现可经设备全局存储写部分结果，再由后续kernel或合适的原子协议合并；这会增加交通与完成边界。存在具备其自身launch/驻留约束的协作执行等其他选择，不能断言无簇时所有组织都只能采用某一协议。另一选择是不拆到多个CTA，直接避免跨CTA部分和，但可能留下并行度不足。真实收益取决于额外交通与所缓解的瓶颈。\\\\n\\\\n片上容量：三级32KiB输入缓冲已占96KiB，在99KiB每block上限下只剩3KiB给其他共享对象，不能再增加完整32KiB一级；在227KiB上容量约束较松，但多分配仍可能降低每SM驻留。缩小Kₜ或减少级数是候选，改变线程数、累加放置与tile则要一起重算寄存器和共享账。延迟隐藏可能来自更多可运行warp、每线程独立工作或异步重叠，不能由CC标签直接判定哪一种占主导。\\\\n\\\\n矩阵指令：固定指南§16.7–16.8区分CC 8.0/8.6/8.7的第三代与8.9/9.0的第四代Tensor Core及其输入格式支持；9.0另有warpgroup范围的异步矩阵机制。具体形状、dtype、布局与工具链入口仍按目标指令核实，不能从“支持FP8”推出任何矩阵API都支持FP8。把Hopper的warpgroup分工改到warp级指令，需要重新安排accumulator持有者、交接与完成范围；改到ROCm的MFMA/LDS或其他平台同理，不能继承32lane与CUDA barrier约定。\\\\n\\\\n这些替代各自的成本可以单独测量：加载指令占比、cp.async 等待空洞、全局交换字节与归约 kernel 时间、占用率上限下的实际驻留。它们是设计轴上的点，不是 8.x 的固定配方；一个在 9.0 上最优的流水在 8.9 上可能被更浅、更小、更多 block 的组织超过。轴上未列点同样合法。\\\\n\\\\n<!-- K-FW-004：编译与动态形状：Guard、分桶和变体成本\\\\n\\\\n编译把一组可证明成立的执行假设变成专门程序；动态服务需要管理这些假设覆盖的形状与状态空间。\\\\n\\\\n## 特化得到什么\\\\n\\\\n编译器可以融合算子、消除中间张量、选择 tile 和简化控制流，这些改进依赖 shape、stride、dtype、常量或其他 guard。guard 失效可能触发重编译或回退。动态 shape 支持让部分维度符号化，但数据相关控制流、固定 workspace 和特定 kernel 仍可能要求静态边界。\\\\n\\\\nbatch size 相同但 stride 不同、长度分布不同或不同 LoRA rank，都可能走不同变体。只记录一个“batch=8”不足以解释编译缓存。形状签名应描述实际引发特化的条件。\\\\n\\\\n## 分桶的优化目标\\\\n\\\\n将长度 n 映射到桶 b≥n，以 padding 换稳定形状。线性工作浪费近似随 b−n，密集 attention 的浪费则与 b²−n² 有关。bucket 越密，运行浪费越小，但编译时间、可执行程序数量、图和 workspace 驻留越多。\\\\n\\\\n可把总成本写为请求分布下的期望执行成本＋摊销编译成本＋驻留资源代价。某个很少出现的长度值得直接 eager，未必值得专门编译。batch、context、query 数、模态网格是联合维度，对每轴独立细分可能产生组合爆炸。\\\\n\\\\n## 一个分桶推导\\\\n\\\\n假设输入多集中在 100–128 和 900–1024，少量到 2048。只用 2048 桶给短输入造成巨大无效工作；按 128、1024、2048 三桶可能大幅减少它。是否增加 256/512 桶取决于真实分布质量，而非照搬二次幂。前缀命中后待算 query 长度还可能与总历史长完全不同，需要分别考虑。\\\\n\\\\n## 与 CUDA Graph 的关系\\\\n\\\\n编译程序处理算子计算，CUDA Graph 处理一段设备命令的重放。动态编译并不自动使图能改变全部地址和拓扑；固定图也可以调用未编译的 kernel。两者组合时，应先明确编译变体和图桶各自的 key，再说明持久缓冲与有效长度如何输入。\\\\n\\\\n冷启动包括模型加载、编译、autotune、图捕获和内存池建立。稳定态测量可以排除这些成本，部署可用性和首次请求目标则必须包含。重新编译频繁会把所谓稳定服务变成持续冷路径，需从 guard 失效原因推导应符号化还是分桶。\\\\n\\\\n## 从模型函数到 IR、lowering 和执行计划\\\\n\\\\n图获取把某次或一组合法执行的算子与依赖变成中间表示。它必须保留张量 shape、stride、dtype、常量、别名与副作用：写 KV、更新随机状态、通信和事件不能仅当作可任意重排的纯函数。数据相关控制流可能留在宿主、分图或通过受支持表示进入编译；图获取成功不证明所有路径均被覆盖。\\\\n\\\\n图级 IR 描述算子之间的数据流，适合常量折叠、代数改写、融合分组和全局布局传播；算子/循环级 IR 描述每个输出元素的索引、归约域和存储位置，适合 tile、向量化、线程绑定及片上数据复用。Lowering 再把这些计划映射成库调用、目标指令与实际内存操作。TVM 固定论文将计算定义、schedule 和硬件 intrinsic 分开，正是为了让同一函数能有多种合法实现。\\\\n\\\\n编译器可以生成同步与缓冲复用，但其证明范围只覆盖所见依赖。服务执行器仍负责选择变体、提供合法输入、保持在途对象寿命，并协调编译区域外的拷贝、调度和状态提交。将异步 copy 放到另一个 stream，却未将事件关系传入执行计划，不会因模型已经编译而变安全。\\\\n\\\\n## 融合与布局传播需要完整消费者关系\\\\n\\\\n以 Y=activation(XW+b) 为例，GEMM 的 epilogue 可在输出尚在寄存器时完成 bias 与激活，避免中间写读。若未激活的 XW 同时有另一消费者，则要保留该值、复制它或改变融合边界。若归约次序、dtype 或饱和点变化，需验证数值契约；不能只由最终张量 shape 相同判断合法。\\\\n\\\\n把权重预打包成某个内核布局，可在模型加载阶段摊销；运行时激活转换通常按请求付费。一个较快算子若要求额外两次布局转换，可能令整段更慢。图级选择应比较整条 producer→consumer 链，包括 residual 分支、外部库边界、别名和最终输出布局。静态内存复用也必须依据最后消费者，异步执行时不能只按宿主调用返回顺序判定结束。\\\\n\\\\n动态尺寸与动态 rank 需要区别。固定 PyTorch 2026-04-30 文档说明动态 shape 以符号维度描述变化，不支持一般的输入 rank 变化；shape 条件分支仍可产生特化。0/1 等特殊尺寸、stride、数据相关输出数量和自定义 kernel 的 constexpr 也可能影响覆盖范围。标记一个维度动态不会自动解除每个 backend 的静态容量要求。\\\\n\\\\n## 编译缓存与在线变体的实际身份\\\\n\\\\n可执行产物应绑定其真实依赖：算子语义和图、目标架构、编译器/库版本、优化及数值选项、shape/stride/dtype guard 和已折叠常量。若权重只是运行时参数且 ABI/布局不变，不必把每个数值变化都当作重新编译理由；若权重已折叠、预打包格式改变或图捕获保存了地址，则要重建对应产物。缓存失效范围应由依赖决定。\\\\n\\\\n编译、autotune、权重打包和 CUDA Graph 捕获产生不同对象，复用 key 及释放条件也不同。清除编译缓存不代表已实例化 graph 不再引用旧缓冲；更换图桶也不保证旧编译 module 可以立即卸载。新模型版本准备与旧请求 drain 期间，要把两套常量、可执行产物与工作区的并存峰值计入。\\\\n\\\\n一个摊销设定：编译与调优共耗 3 s，每次合法调用节省 0.05 ms，至少需 60,000 次调用才能仅从总计算时间回本；这还未计额外驻留和首请求等待。少见形状可以采用受验证的通用路径，高频形状值得特化。若初始小样本未覆盖长尾，在线不断生成新变体会同时消耗主机与设备资源，应根据实际变体分布重新设计符号范围和桶，而非无限扩大缓存。\\\\n\\\\n## 搜索、回退与验证共同约束编译优化\\\\n\\\\nAnsor 固定论文通过结构草图、细节参数和硬件测量搜索完整张量程序，并把调优预算偏向影响端到端成本的子图。这给 InfraAgents 的设计探索提供一个具体启示：成本模型用于选下一批实验，不能代替合法性与目标硬件测量；局部子图最快也不自动意味着服务尾延迟最佳。\\\\n\\\\n验证至少覆盖 guard 边界内外、非连续输入、别名、特殊尺寸、不同 batch 组成、首次与重复调用，以及更新模型后的缓存命中。保存参考函数并比较分段边界，遇到差异可定位到哪次改写/精度选择。回退路径必须执行相同任务语义，并记录发生条件和占比；静默改变 mask、截断输出或绕开质量约束不属于合法回退。\\\\n\\\\n最终测量包含运行时转换、计划生成、冷编译和长时间变体增长。固定形状、大量复用且融合节省中间流量时，专门编译更有利；高度动态、外部状态多、成熟库已接近瓶颈上限或部署寿命短时，部分编译或直接库调用可能更合适。\\\\n\\\\n<!-- infraagents:provenance -->\\\\n\\\\n## \\\"source_original\\\", \\\"content\\\": \\\"\\\\n===== nki/guides/architecture/trainium2_arch.rst =====\\\\n.. meta::\\\\n   :description: Trainium2 Architecture Guide for NKI\\\\n   :keywords: AWS Neuron, Trainium2, NeuronCore-v3, NKI, architecture\\\\n   :date-modified: 12/01/2025\\\\n\\\\n.. _trainium2_arch:\\\\n\\\\nTrainium2 Architecture Guide for NKI\\\\n===============================================\\\\n\\\\nIn this guide, we will dive into hardware architecture of third-generation NeuronDevices: Trainium2. This guide will highlight major architectural updates compared to the previous generation. Therefore, we assume readers have gone through :doc:`Trainium/Inferentia2 Architecture Guide </nki/guides/architecture/trainium_inferentia2_arch>` in detail to understand the basics of NeuronDevice Architecture.\\\\n\\\\nThe diagram below shows a block diagram of a Trainium2 device, which consists of:\\\\n\\\\n* 8 NeuronCores (v3).\\\\n* 4 HBM stacks with a total device memory capacity of 96GiB and bandwidth of 3TB/s.\\\\n* 128 DMA (Direct Memory Access) engines to move data within and across devices.\\\\n* 20 CC-Cores for collective communication.\\\\n* 4 NeuronLink-v3 for device-to-device collective communication.\\\\n\\\\n.. _fig-arch-neuron-device-v3:\\\\n\\\\n.. image:: /nki/img/arch_images/neuron_device3.png\\\\n\\\\nTrainium2 Device Diagram.\\\\n\\\\nFor a high-level architecture specification comparison from Trainium1 to Trainium2, check out the\\\\n:doc:`Neuron architecture guide for Trainium2 </about-neuron/arch/neuron-hardware/trainium2>`. The rest of this guide will provide details on new features or improvements in NeuronCore-v3 compute engines and memory subsystem compared to NeuronCore-v2.\\\\n\\\\nNeuronCore-v3 Compute Engine Updates\\\\n------------------------------------\\\\n\\\\nThe figure below is a simplified NeuronCore-v3 diagram of the compute engines and their connectivity to the two on-chip SRAMs, SBUF and PSUM. This is similar to NeuronCore-v2.\\\\n\\\\n.. _fig-neuroncore-v3-diagram:\\\\n\\\\n.. image:: /nki/img/arch_images/nki-trn2-arch-1.png\\\\n\\\\nNeuronCore-v3 SBUF capacity is **28MiB** (or, 128 partitions of 224KiB), up from 24 MiB in NeuronCore-v2. PSUM capacity remains the same at 2MiB. Engine data-path width and frequency are updated to the following:\\\\n\\\\n.. list-table:: Compute Engine Specifications\\\\n   :widths: 20 20 40 20\\\\n   :header-rows: 1\\\\n\\\\n   * - Device Architecture\\\\n     - Compute Engine\\\\n     - Data-path Width (elements/cycle)\\\\n     - Frequency (GHz)\\\\n   * - Trainium2\\\\n     - Tensor\\\\n     - 4x128 (dense FP8_E4/FP8_E5 input), 2x128 (dense BF16/FP16 input) or 5x128 (sparse input); 1x128 (output)\\\\n     - 2.4\\\\n   * - \\\\n     - Vector\\\\n     - 512 BF16/FP16 input/output; 256 input/output for other data types\\\\n     - 0.96\\\\n   * - \\\\n     - Scalar\\\\n     - 128 input/output\\\\n     - 1.2\\\\n   * - \\\\n     - GpSimd\\\\n     - \\\\n     - 1.2\\\\n\\\\nNext, we will go over major updates to each compute engine.\\\\n\\\\nTensor Engine\\\\n--------------\\\\n\\\\nThe Tensor Engine is optimized for tensor computations such as GEMM, CONV, and Transpose. A NeuronCore-v3 Tensor Engine delivers 158 FP8, 79 BF16/FP16/TF32 and 20 FP32 dense TFLOPS of tensor computations. It also delivers 316 FP8/BF16/FP16/TF32 sparse TFLOPS. The rest of this section describes new architectural features introduced in NeuronCore-v3 Tensor Engine. \\\\n\\\\nDouble FP8 Matmul Performance\\\\n^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^\\\\n\\\\nNeuronCore-v3 TensorEngine (TensorE from now on) supports matrix multiplications (matmuls) of FP8 input matrices (including FP8_E4 and FP8_E5 formats [1]_) at **double** the throughput compared to BF16/FP16. Mixing FP8_E4 in one input matrix and FP8_E5 in the other is also allowed. This FP8 double performance mode uses FP32 as the accumulation data type, similar to BF16/FP16 matmul.\\\\n\\\\n.. [1] FP8_E3 format is still supported by NeuronCore-v3 TensorE similar to NeuronCore-v2, but its matmul performance is the same as BF16/FP16.\\\\n\\\\nLogically, TensorE doubles the FP8 matmul performance by doubling the maximum contraction dimension of a matmul instruction from 128 (for BF16/FP16) to 256, effectively presenting a 256x128 systolic array to the programmer. Under the hood, since the systolic array is still organized as a grid of 128x128 processing elements, each processing element performs two pairs of FP8 multiplications and also accumulation of the two multiplication results per cycle. The remaining section discusses the semantics of a single double-FP8 matmul instruction. Multiple such instructions can be used to accommodate larger matrix multiplications than the allowed instruction-level tile sizes.\\\\n\\\\nA double-FP8 matmul can perform a multiplication of a 128x256 matrix and a 256x512 matrix (that is, MxKxN matmul, M=128, K=256, N=512). The figure below shows a visualization of the two input matrices (x and y) and the matmul output matrix (output). The figure also highlights two elements (red and yellow) in the first row of the x matrix and in the first column of the y matrix. These two elements are 128 (K//2) elements apart within the rows and columns. We will use these elements to illustrate the SBUF layout requirements for these matrices next. \\\\n\\\\n\\\\n.. _fig-double-fp8-matmul:\\\\n\\\\n.. image:: /nki/img/arch_images/nki-trn2-arch-2.png\\\\n\\\\nThese tensors must still fit in the 128-partition SBUF, with each partition feeding data into each row of processing elements inside the TensorE. The contraction of size 256 is therefore split into two dimensions: (1) the partition dimension of size 128 and (2) the most major (slowest) free dimension of size 2. This is illustrated in the figure below. Both the stationary matrix (x in above figure) and the moving matrix (y in above figure) are sliced in two tiles, where the first and second tile correspond to first and second halves of the contraction dimension, respectively. \\\\n\\\\n.. _fig-double-fp8-sbuf-layout:\\\\n\\\\n.. image:: /nki/img/arch_images/nki-trn2-arch-3.png\\\\n\\\\nNext, we invoke the LoadStationary and MultiplyMoving instructions to perform the matrix multiplications using the above tensors in SBUF. This is illustrated in figure below. The LoadStationary instruction loads the stationary tensor (K/2=128, 2, M=128) into TensorE, which stores two data elements into a single processing element (for example, the red and yellow elements land in the first processing element of TensorE as shown in ❶). Next, the MultiplyMoving instruction streams the moving tensor horizontally across the loaded stationary tensor. Similar to LoadStationary, two elements of moving tensor are sent to the same processing element simultaneously as shown in ❷, such that they can get multiplied with the corresponding pair of loaded stationary elements.\\\\n\\\\n.. _fig-double-fp8-instruction:\\\\n\\\\n.. image:: /nki/img/arch_images/nki-trn2-arch-4.png\\\\n\\\\nNote that the above double FP8 ``LoadStationary``/``MultiplyMoving`` instruction sequence with a 256 contraction dimension takes the same amount of time as the regular BF16/FP16 LoadStationary/MultiplyMoving instruction sequence with a 128 contraction dimension. Since the double FP8 instruction performs double the FLOPs, overall double FP8 matmul on TensorE can achieve double the throughput compared to BF16/FP16 matmuls.\\\\n\\\\nNKI programmers can invoke double FP8 matmul using the ``nisa.nc_matmul()`` API on NeuronCore-v3:\\\\n\\\\n.. code-block:: python\\\\n\\\\n   import nki.isa as nisa\\\\n\\\\n   # stationary: [128, 2, 128]\\\\n   # moving: [128, 2, 512]\\\\n   # dst: [128, 512]\\\\n   nisa.nc_matmul(dst, stationary, moving, \\\\n                  perf_mode=nisa.matmul_perf_mode.double_row, ...)\\\\n\\\\nThe ``nt.tensor[128, 2, 128]`` stationary and ``nt.tensor[128, 2, 512]`` moving tensor shapes reflect the maximum tile sizes for the double FP8 matmul instruction. Smaller tile sizes are supported, though the second dimension (the most major free dimension) of both input tensors must be two. In other words, if the contraction dimension of the matmul is not a multiple of two, programmers are required to explicitly pad the input tensors with zeros to enable the performance mode.\\\\n\\\\nNote that Double FP8 matmul performance mode cannot be combined with the following TensorE features:\\\\n\\\\n* Column tiling mode\\\\n* Sparse matmul (new in NeuronCore-v3, discussion below)\\\\n* Transpose mode (new in NeuronCore-v3, more discussion below)\\\\n\\\\n.. TODO: Uncomment and unindent when the NISA API ships\\\\n   M:N Structured Sparsity\\\\n   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^\\\\n\\\\n   Trainium2 TensorE introduces sparse matmul (matrix multiplication) support for M:N structured sparsity. This new functionality multiplies a regular dense moving matrix with a sparse stationary matrix that exhibits a M:N sparsity pattern, where every N elements only have up to M non-zero values along the contraction dimension. Trainium2 hardware supports up to 4x compression ratio and therefore 4x faster matmul performance compared to dense, with the largest value of N being 16. Programmers also have the flexibility to choose a lower compression ratio (CR=N/M) for better model accuracy. NKI currently supports the following M:N patterns: 4:8 (2x compression), 4:12 (3x) and 4:16 (4x), through the ``nki.isa.sparse_matmul`` API.\\\\n\\\\n   To exercise sparse matmul, the sparse stationary matrix must be compressed to store only M out of every N elements, along with a tag tensor which indicates the original positions of the remaining M non-zero elements. In Figure below, a stationary matrix with a compression ratio of 16:4, along with its compressed representation.\\\\n\\\\n   .. _fig-sparse-matmul:\\\\n\\\\n   .. image:: /nki/img/arch_images/nki-trn2-arch-5.png\\\\n\\\\n   The ``nki.isa.sparse_matmul`` API takes the following arguments ``nc_matmul_sparse(moving, stationary, tag, compress_ratio)``.\\\\n\\\\n   Each row TensorE is able to read from 4, 2, or 1 SBUF partitions corresponding to the maximum compression ratio supported by the sparsity on TRN2 ratio. In order to efficiently utilize the TensorE the input moving should have shape ``[Partition Dimension <=128, Compression Ratio, Tile Free Dimension <= 512]``. The stationary matrix represents a 128x128 compressed weight tensor.\\\\n\\\\n   Finally, the tag tensor is a 128x32 tensor of uint16. Each position of uncompressed elements is encoded as an 4-bit integer, which is the minimal width to relative position within N=16. Four tags are then packed into a uint16 datatype which forms the [128,32] tensor.\\\\n\\\\n   A sample ``nki.isa.sparse_matmul`` can be found here:\\\\n\\\\n   .. code-block:: python\\\\n\\\\n      def mm_sparse_128_512_cr4(moving_tensor, stationary_tensor, tag_tensor, output):\\\\n      \\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\n      Args:\\\\n         moving: Input tensor of shape [128, 4, 512], which represents activation tensor\\\\n         stationary: Input tensor of shape [128, 128], which represents the \\\\n                     compressed weight tensor\\\\n         tag: Input tensor of shape [128, 32] of uint16 datatype where each tag \\\\n               represents the indices of non-zero elements of the weight tensor.\\\\n               Tags are uint4 datatypes, 4 tags are packed into 1 uint16 datatype\\\\n         output: reference to the resulting output tensor of shape [128, 512]\\\\n      \\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\n      _, compress_ratio, _ = moving_tensor.shape\\\\n      \\\\n      moving = nl.ndarray(moving_tensor.shape, dtype=moving_tensor.dtype, buffer=nl.sbuf)\\\\n      stationary = nl.ndarray(stationary_tensor.shape, dtype=stationary_tensor.dtype, buffer=nl.sbuf)\\\\n      tag = nl.ndarray(tag_tensor.shape, dtype=tag_tensor.dtype, buffer=nl.sbuf)\\\\n      nisa.dma_copy(dst=moving, src=moving_tensor)\\\\n      nisa.dma_copy(dst=stationary, src=stationary_tensor)\\\\n      nisa.dma_copy(dst=tag, src=tag_tensor)\\\\n\\\\n      psum_buf = nc_matmul_sparse(moving, # [128P, 4, 512F] \\\\n                                    stationary, # [128P, 128F]\\\\n                                    tag, # [128, 32]\\\\n                                    compress_ratio)\\\\n\\\\n      nisa.dma_copy(dst=output, src=psum_buf)\\\\n\\\\n      # Sparse matmul     \\\\n      def test_nc_matmul_sparse(self):\\\\n         M = 512\\\\n         N = 128\\\\n         K = 128\\\\n         sparsity_pattern = (16, 4)\\\\n         L, R = sparsity_pattern\\\\n         ratio = L // R\\\\n\\\\n         moving = np.random.random_sample((K, ratio, M)).astype(dtype) # activation\\\\n         stationary = np.random.random_sample((K, N)).astype(dtype) # compressed weight \\\\n         \\\\n         # For demonstration purpose, we use random values between 0~15 in the tag tensor\\\\n         tag = np.random.randint(0, 16, size=(K, N), dtype=np.ubyte)\\\\n         \\\\n         # maps logical tags to physical tags and pack 4 uint4 to 1 uint\\\\n         squeezed_tag = squeeze_tags(tag, ratio) \\\\n         \\\\n         # Generate NKI output\\\\n         nki_output = np.zeros((N, M), dtype=dtype)\\\\n         mm_sparse_128_512_cr4(moving, stationary, squeezed_tag, nki_output)\\\\n\\\\nBuilt-in Transpose Support\\\\n^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^\\\\n\\\\nAs discussed in :doc:`Trainium/Inferentia2 Architecture Guide </nki/guides/architecture/trainium_inferentia2_arch>`, one common use of TensorE besides matrix multiplication operations is transposition of a 2D SBUF tensor, which swaps the partition and free dimension of the matrix. Such a transposition is done through a matmul of the tensor to be transposed (stationary tensor) and an identity matrix (moving tensor). Prior to NeuronCore-v3, TensorE has to perform multiplication of each data element with 1.0 or 0.0 and accumulation along the contraction dimension normally. However, if the tensor to be transposed contains NaN/Inf floating point values, the matmul result will not be a bit-accurate transposition of the original matrix - the NaN/Inf values will propagate through the accumulation chain and spread across the output tensor.\\\\n\\\\nStarting with NeuronCore-v3, TensorE supports an explicit transpose mode, which can correctly transpose input tensors with NaN/Inf. In addition, the transpose mode provides the following benefits:\\\\n\\\\n* 2x speedup in FP32 transpose, vs. no transpose mode enabled.\\\\n* FP16/BF16 PSUM output for FP16/BF16 transpose, vs. FP32 (default matmul output data type) PSUM output when no transpose mode enabled. This allows faster PSUM data eviction back to SBUF.\\\\n\\\\n.. note:: NeuronCore-v3 TensorE transpose mode for FP8 input data produces 16-bit output elements in PSUM, with the upper 8 bits filled with zeros.\\\\n\\\\nNKI programmers can enable TensorE transpose mode on NeuronCore-v3 through the following APIs:\\\\n\\\\n.. code-block:: python\\\\n\\\\n   nisa.nc_matmul(..., is_transpose=True)\\\\n   # OR\\\\n   nisa.nc_transpose(..., engine=nisa.constants.engine.tensor)\\\\n\\\\nVector Engine\\\\n----------------\\\\n\\\\nVector Engine (VectorE) is specially designed to accelerate vector operations where every element in the output tensor typically depends on multiple elements from input tensor(s), such as vector reduction and element-wise operators between two tensors. NeuronCore-v3 Vector Engine delivers a total of 1.0 TFLOPS of FP32 computations and can handle various input/output data-types, including FP8, FP16, BF16, TF32, FP32, INT8, INT16, and INT32. \\\\n\\\\nVector Engine Performance Mode\\\\n^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^\\\\n\\\\nNeuronCore-v3 Vector Engine provides a new performance mode BF16/FP16 data types, which quadruples or doubles the instruction throughput depending on the instruction type compared to NeuronCore-v2 (more details below). Enabling this performance mode does not change the computation precision - all computation is still done in FP32, similar to NeuronCore-v2 Vector Engine.\\\\n\\\\nIn particular, the following instructions could see a 4x throughput lift compared to NeuronCore-v2:\\\\n\\\\n1. ``nisa.tensor_copy`` and ``nisa.tensor_scalar`` when both input/output tensors:\\\\n    a. are in SBUF\\\\n    b. are in BF16/FP16 (input and output data types do not need to match)\\\\n    c. have physically contiguous elements in the inner-most (most minor) free dimension\\\\n\\\\nThe following instructions could see a 2x throughput lift compared to NeuronCore-v2:\\\\n\\\\n1. ``nisa.tensor_copy`` and ``nisa.tensor_scalar``:\\\\n    a. when both input/output tensors satisfy 1a and 1b, but not 1c conditions above, or\\\\n    b. when both input/output tensors satisfy 1b and 1c, but one of input and output tensors is in PSUM\\\\n2. ``nisa.tensor_tensor``:\\\\n    a. when both input tensors are SBUF and all of input/output tensors are in BF16/FP16\\\\n\\\\nNote, NKI programmers are not required to explicitly enable VectorE performance mode. VectorE detects the above conditions and enables performance mode automatically in hardware.\\\\n\\\\nScalar Engine\\\\n---------------\\\\n\\\\nAs discussed in Trainium/Inferentia2 Architecture Guide, Scalar Engine (ScalarE) is specially designed to accelerate scalar operations where every element in the output tensor only depends on one element of the input tensor. In addition, ScalarE provides hardware acceleration to evaluate non-linear functions such as Gelu and Sqrt. All architectural capabilities from NeuronCore-v2 Scalar Engine are applicable to NeuronCore-v3. NeuronCore-v3 Scalar Engine additionally supports bit-accurate tensor copies without intermediate FP32 data type casting, similar to VectorE and Gpsimd Engine (see details in ``nisa.tensor_copy``).\\\\n\\\\nGpsimd Engine\\\\n--------------\\\\n\\\\nGpSimd Engine (GpSimdE) is intended to be a general-purpose engine that can run any ML operators that cannot be lowered onto the other highly specialized compute engines discussed above efficiently, such as applying a triangular mask to a tensor. A GpSimdE consists of eight fully programmable processors that can execute arbitrary C/C++ programs.\\\\n\\\\nIn NeuronCore-v3, each processor in GpsimdE also comes with an integrated DMA engine that can move data in parallel to computation on GpsimdE and also parallel to data movements done by the main DMA engines on the Neuron Device. These integrated DMA engines can reach any SBUF/HBM on-chip or off-chip in the same trn2 instance. All eight processors together have a total integrated DMA bandwidth of 307 GB/s (153 GB/s per read/write direction).\\\\n\\\\nIn NeuronCore-v3, each processor in GpsimdE also comes with an integrated DMA engine that can move data in parallel to computation on GpsimdE and also parallel to data movements done by the main DMA engines on the Neuron Device. These integrated DMA engines can reach any SBUF/HBM on-chip or off-chip in the same trn2 instance. All eight processors together have a total integrated DMA bandwidth of 307 GB/s (153 GB/s per read/write direction). \\\\n\\\\nData Movement Updates\\\\n----------------------\\\\n\\\\nTrainium2 consists of a three-tiered memory hierarchy: HBM, SBUF and PSUM, from highest to lowest memory capacity. Figures below show the specifications of these memories and their connectivity for one NeuronCore-v3.\\\\n\\\\n.. _fig-memory-hierarchy:\\\\n\\\\n.. image:: /nki/img/arch_images/nki-trn2-arch-5-1.png\\\\n\\\\n.. _fig-memory-hierarchy-2:\\\\n\\\\n.. image:: /nki/img/arch_images/nki-trn2-arch-6.png\\\\n\\\\nAs shown in the above figures, data movement between HBM and SBUF is performed using on-chip DMA (Direct Memory Access) engines, which can run in parallel to computation within the NeuronCore. Data movement between PSUM and SBUF is done through ISA instructions on the compute engines. In NeuronCore-v3, two restrictions in engine parallel accesses to SBUF/PSUM are lifted to improve programming flexibility compared to NeuronCore-v2:\\\\n\\\\n1. VectorE and GpSimdE can access SBUF in parallel.\\\\n    a. This was disallowed in NeuronCore-v2.\\\\n    b. VectorE's performance mode leverages a shared memory bus between the VectorE and GpsimdE engines to deliver 2-4x performance improvement for select VectorE instructions. The hardware automatically coordinates access between engines to optimize bus utilization, including arbitrating between GpsimdE and relevant VectorE instructions.\\\\n2. VectorE and ScalarE can access PSUM in parallel.\\\\n    a. This was disallowed in NeuronCore-v2.\\\\n    b. Both VectorE and ScalarE can access PSUM at full bandwidth in parallel, as long as their accesses do not collide on the same PSUM bank.\\\\n\\\\nDMA Transpose\\\\n^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^\\\\n\\\\nTrainium2 DMA engines can perform a tensor transpose while moving data from HBM into SBUF, or from SBUF to SBUF itself. The figure below illustrates these two supported DMA transpose data flows. Trainium2 DMA transpose supports bit-accurate transposition for both 2-byte and 4-byte data types.\\\\n\\\\n.. _fig-dma-transpose:\\\\n\\\\n.. image:: /nki/img/arch_images/nki-trn2-arch-7.png\\\\n\\\\nHBM2SBUF DMA transpose\\\\n\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\n\\\\nBefore diving into how HBM2SBUF transpose works, let's revisit a simple DMA copy from a packed HBM tensor ``[128, 512]`` to an SBUF tensor ``[nl.par_dim(128), 512]``. Following Numpy convention, these tensor shapes follow a major to minor ordering. The figure below visualizes these HBM and SBUF tensors. A packed ``[128, 512]`` HBM tensor consists of 128 chunks of 512 elements, laid out back to back in the HBM linear memory. The most minor (that is, inner-most) dimension consists of 512 contiguous elements in memory. Once loaded into the SBUF, the most minor HBM tensor dimension (512) is mapped to the free dimension of the SBUF, while the most major dimension is mapped to the SBUF partition dimension.\\\\n\\\\nIn Trainium2, each NeuronCore-v3 is typically paired with 16x DMA engines to drive its corresponding SBUF bandwidth. In the above DMA copy, each DMA engine would be responsible for moving 128/16 = 8 chunks of 512 elements.\\\\n\\\\n* HBM tensor [128, 512]: 512 is the inner-most (minor) dimension\\\\n\\\\n.. _fig-hbm2sbuf-dma-copy:\\\\n\\\\n.. image:: /nki/img/arch_images/nki-trn2-arch-8.png\\\\n\\\\nIn contrast, in a DMA transpose operation, we take an HBM tensor of opposite layout [512, 128]:\\\\n\\\\n.. _fig-hbm2sbuf-dma-transpose:\\\\n\\\\n.. image:: /nki/img/arch_images/nki-trn2-arch-9.png\\\\n\\\\nIn a DMA transposition, the most minor dimension of the source HBM tensor now becomes the partition dimension of the SBUF in destination. Compared to the above DMA copy operation where each DMA engine reads and writes an independent slice of 512 elements, DMA transpose requires all 16x DMA engines to work co-operatively to deliver the best throughput - these 16x DMA engines should write into a single ``[nl.par_dim(128), 16]`` SBUF tile in parallel at a time, where the 16 elements along free dimension must be contiguous. Having a multiple of 128 and a multiple of 16 in the output SBUF partition and inner-most free dimension sizes is a pre-requisite to achieve best DMA throughput efficiency possible with DMA transpose. However, it is not a functionality requirement - DMA transpose can flexible tile sizes for DMA transpose at the cost of DMA performance. \\\\n\\\\nHBM2SBUF DMA transpose is commonly seen in ML workloads where the data layout in HBM differs from the format needed by the initial compute engine that processes the data. For example, in the LLM decode phase, the K cache typically has an HBM layout of ``[seqlen, d_head]``, where ``seqlen`` and ``d_head`` are the sequence length and head dimensions respectively. However, when K is consumed by TensorE in the Q@K operator in self-attention, ``d_head`` is the contraction dimension of the matrix multiplication. Therefore, the most-minor d_head dimension in HBM should become the partition dimension to satisfy TensorE layout requirements (see :ref:`Tiling <nki-tile-layout>`: Contraction dimension must map to partition dimension). Mapping most minor HBM tensor dimension to SBUF partition dimension is exactly an HBM2SBUF DMA transpose operation on Trainium2. \\\\n\\\\nIn NKI, programmers can invoke an HBM2SBUF DMA transpose using the ``nisa.dma_transpose`` API.\\\\n\\\\n.. code-block:: python\\\\n\\\\n   import nki\\\\n   import nki.language as nl\\\\n   import nki.isa as nisa\\\\n\\\\n   # hbm_src: [512, 128] in shared_hbm\\\\n   sbuf_dst = nl.ndarray((128, 512), dtype=hbm_src.dtype, buffer=nl.sbuf)\\\\n   nisa.dma_transpose(dst=sbuf_dst, src=hbm_src)\\\\n\\\\n.. admonition:: Performance Consideration\\\\n\\\\n   DMA transpose on Trainium2 can achieve up to 90% DMA throughput utilization given hardware-friendly tensor access patterns, compared to up to 100% throughput utilization for a DMA copy.\\\\n\\\\nSBUF2SBUF DMA transpose\\\\n\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\n\\\\nSBUF2SBUF DMA transpose works in a similar fashion as HBM2SBUF transpose, where the most minor dimension of the input SBUF tensor, i.e., inner-most free dimension, becomes the partition dimension of the output SBUF tensor. Therefore, SBUF2SBUF DMA transpose is a way to swap partition and free axis of an SBUF tensor, an alternative to TensorE transpose.\\\\n\\\\nThe same ``nisa.dma_transpose`` API can be used to perform an SBUF2SBUF DMA transpose:\\\\n\\\\n.. code-block:: python\\\\n\\\\n   import nki\\\\n   import nki.language as nl\\\\n   import nki.isa as nisa\\\\n\\\\n   # sbuf_src: [128, 128] in sbuf\\\\n   sbuf_dst = nl.ndarray((128, 128), dtype=sbuf_src.dtype, buffer=nl.sbuf)\\\\n   nisa.dma_transpose(dst=sbuf_dst, src=sbuf_src)\\\\n\\\\nPerformance Consideration. SBUF2SBUF transpose can achieve up to 50% of DMA throughput on Trainium2. Compared to TensorE transpose that is more performant but requires ScalarE/VectorE to evict the transposed output from PSUM back to SBUF, DMA transpose can read from and write to SBUF directly. Therefore, DMA transpose is particularly useful in operators that are ScalarE/VectorE bound, such as self attention.\\\\n\\\\n.. _dge_arch:\\\\n\\\\nDescriptor Generation Engine (DGE)\\\\n^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^\\\\n\\\\nThe Descriptor Generation Engine (DGE) is a new hardware block in NeuronCore-v3 that accelerates DMA descriptor generation to perform either DMA copy or transpose on the DMA engines. Each NeuronCore-v3 comes with two instances of DGE, which can be commanded through either SyncE or ScalarE sequencer. The figure below shows the connectivity of the DGE instances.\\\\n\\\\n.. _fig-dge:\\\\n\\\\n.. image:: /nki/img/arch_images/nki-trn2-arch-10.png\\\\n\\\\nPrior to Trainium2, DMA descriptor generation was handled in two ways. They were either generated statically on the host when loading a NEFF onto a Neuron Device (i.e., static DMA), or created dynamically through custom kernels on GpsimdE during NEFF execution (i.e., software DGE). The static approach stored all descriptors in HBM, consuming valuable memory space that could otherwise be used for model parameters or computation data. The software-based approach used a portion of SBUF for storing descriptors generated during execution and occupies GpsimdE that could otherwise perform useful computation.\\\\n\\\\nIn comparison, the new hardware-based DGE in Trainium2 generates descriptors on demand without requiring additional memory storage. It also frees up GpsimdE to perform useful computation. Therefore, it is recommended to leverage hardware-based DGE on Trainium2 whenever possible to initiate a DMA transfer.\\\\n\\\\nNKI programmers can invoke hardware-based DGE on NeuronCore-v3 using ``nisa.dma_copy`` and ``nisa.dma_transpose`` APIs, by setting ``dge_mode=nisa.dge_mode.hw_dge``. The compute engine to initiate a DGE command (Sync Engine or ScalarE) is currently determined by NKI compiler (subject to changes).\\\\n\\\\n.. note::\\\\n   NeuronCore-v3 hardware DGE currently does not support indirect DMA operations (gather/scatter). Refer to nisa API documentation for detailed implementation guidelines.\\\\n\\\\n.. admonition:: Performance Consideration\\\\n\\\\n   When triggered from ScalarE, execution of the DGE-based DMA instruction could be hidden behind earlier compute instructions (such as ``nisa.activate()``) in program order, since DGE and the compute pipeline of ScalarE are independent hardware resources. Each DGE-based DMA instruction takes about 600 ns to execute on NeuronCore-v3.\\\\n\\\\n\\\", \\\"excerpt_ranges\\\": [[0, 27103]], \\\"range_unit\\\": \\\"zero-based half-open characters in extracted text\\\", \\\"extracted_characters\\\": 27103, \\\"selected_characters\\\": 27103, \\\"extraction\\\": \\\"UTF-8 text\\\", \\\"selection_reason\\\": \\\"full extracted text fits allocation\\\"}, {\\\"path\\\": \\\"references/S-FLASH/fulltext.txt\\\", \\\"sha256\\\": \\\"8ba7ee7aa00c564a06a7b579777d51896945ba5b179b0ae2ab976fa15decd8bc\\\", \\\"reading_scope\\\": \\\"full\\\", \\\"category\\\": \\\"source_original\\\", \\\"content\\\": \\\"--- PAGE 1 ---\\\\nFlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Eﬃcient Exact Attention\\\\nwith IO-Awareness\\\\nTri Dao†, Daniel Y. Fu†, Stefano Ermon†, Atri Rudra‡, and Christopher Ré†\\\\n†Department of Computer Science, Stanford University\\\\n‡Department of Computer Science and Engineering, University at Buﬀalo, SUNY\\\\n{trid,danfu}@cs.stanford.edu, ermon@stanford.edu, atri@buffalo.edu,\\\\nchrismre@cs.stanford.edu\\\\nJune 24, 2022\\\\nAbstract\\\\nTransformers are slow and memory-hungry on long sequences, since the time and memory complexity\\\\nof self-attention are quadratic in sequence length. Approximate attention methods have attempted\\\\nto address this problem by trading oﬀmodel quality to reduce the compute complexity, but often do\\\\nnot achieve wall-clock speedup. We argue that a missing principle is making attention algorithms IO-\\\\naware—accounting for reads and writes between levels of GPU memory. We propose FlashAttention,\\\\nan IO-aware exact attention algorithm that uses tiling to reduce the number of memory reads/writes\\\\nbetween GPU high bandwidth memory (HBM) and GPU on-chip SRAM. We analyze the IO complexity\\\\nof FlashAttention, showing that it requires fewer HBM accesses than standard attention, and is\\\\noptimal for a range of SRAM sizes. Transformers have grown larger [5] and deeper [83], but\\\\nequipping them with longer context remains diﬃcult [80], since the self-attention module at their heart\\\\nhas time and memory complexity quadratic in sequence length. An important question is whether making\\\\nattention faster and more memory-eﬃcient can help Transformer models address their runtime and memory\\\\nchallenges for long sequences.\\\\nMany approximate attention methods have aimed to reduce the compute and memory requirements of\\\\nattention. These methods range from sparse-approximation [51, 74] to low-rank approximation [12, 50, 84],\\\\nand their combinations [3, 9, 92]. Although these methods reduce the compute requirements to linear or\\\\nnear-linear in sequence length, many of them do not display wall-clock speedup against standard attention\\\\nand have not gained wide adoption. One main reason is that they focus on FLOP reduction (which may not\\\\ncorrelate with wall-clock speed) and tend to ignore overheads from memory access (IO).\\\\nIn this paper, we argue that a missing principle is making attention algorithms IO-aware [1]—that is,\\\\ncarefully accounting for reads and writes to diﬀerent levels of fast and slow memory (e.g., between fast GPU\\\\non-chip SRAM and relatively slow GPU high bandwidth memory, or HBM [45], Figure 1 left). On modern\\\\n1\\\\narXiv:2205.14135v2  [cs.LG]  23 Jun 2022\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 2 ---\\\\nFlashAttention\\\\nMemory Hierarchy with\\\\nBandwidth & Memory Size\\\\nAttention on GPT-2\\\\nFlashAttention\\\\nPyTorch\\\\nTime (ms)\\\\nMatmul\\\\nMask\\\\nSoftmax\\\\nDropout\\\\nMatmul\\\\nFused\\\\nKernel\\\\nQ: N x d\\\\nV: N X d\\\\nKT: d x N\\\\nQKT: N x N\\\\nsm(QKT)V: N x d\\\\nOuter Loop\\\\nCopy Block to SRAM\\\\nCopy\\\\nOuter Loop\\\\nCopy\\\\nInner Loop\\\\nCompute Block\\\\non SRAM\\\\nOutput to HBM\\\\nInner Loop\\\\nInner Loop\\\\nOuter Loop\\\\nGPU\\\\nSRAM\\\\nGPU\\\\nHBM\\\\nMain Memory\\\\n(CPU DRAM)\\\\nSRAM: 19 TB/s (20 MB)\\\\nHBM: 1.5 TB/s (40 GB)\\\\nDRAM: 12.8 GB/s\\\\n                (>1 TB)\\\\n0\\\\n5\\\\n10\\\\n15\\\\nFigure 1: Left: FlashAttention uses tiling to prevent materialization of the large 𝑁× 𝑁attention matrix\\\\n(dotted box) on (relatively) slow GPU HBM. IO-aware algorithms have been critical for similar memory-bound\\\\noperations, when reading and writing data can account for a large portion of the runtime—such as database\\\\njoins [71], image processing [70], numerical linear algebra [4], and more [40, 85]. However, common Python\\\\ninterfaces to deep learning such as PyTorch and Tensorﬂow do not allow ﬁne-grained control of memory\\\\naccess.\\\\nWe propose FlashAttention, a new attention algorithm that computes exact attention with far fewer\\\\nmemory accesses. Our main goal is to avoid reading and writing the attention matrix to and from HBM.\\\\nThis requires (i) computing the softmax reduction without access to the whole input (ii) not storing the large\\\\nintermediate attention matrix for the backward pass. We apply two well-established techniques to address\\\\nthese challenges. (i) We restructure the attention computation to split the input into blocks and make several\\\\npasses over input blocks, thus incrementally performing the softmax reduction (also known as tiling). (ii) We\\\\nstore the softmax normalization factor from the forward pass to quickly recompute attention on-chip in the\\\\nbackward pass, which is faster than the standard approach of reading the intermediate attention matrix from\\\\nHBM. We implement FlashAttention in CUDA to achieve ﬁne-grained control over memory access and\\\\nfuse all the attention operations into one GPU kernel. Even with the increased FLOPs due to recomputation,\\\\nour algorithm both runs faster (up to 7.6x on GPT-2 [67], Figure 1 right) and uses less memory—linear\\\\nin sequence length—than standard attention, thanks to the massively reduced amount of HBM access.\\\\nWe analyze the IO complexity [1] of FlashAttention, proving that it requires 𝑂(𝑁2𝑑2𝑀−1) HBM\\\\naccesses where 𝑑is the head dimension and 𝑀is the size of SRAM, as compared to Ω(𝑁𝑑+ 𝑁2) of standard\\\\nattention. For typical values of 𝑑and 𝑀, FlashAttention requires many times fewer HBM accesses\\\\ncompared to standard attention (up to 9× fewer, as shown in Fig. 2). Moreover, we provide a lower bound,\\\\nshowing that no exact attention algorithm can asymptotically improve on the number of HBM accesses over\\\\nall SRAM sizes.\\\\nWe also show that FlashAttention can serve as a useful primitive for realizing the potential of\\\\napproximate attention algorithms by overcoming their issues with memory access overhead. As a proof of\\\\nconcept, we implement block-sparse FlashAttention, a sparse attention algorithm that is 2-4× faster than\\\\neven FlashAttention, scaling up to sequence length of 64k. We prove that block-sparse FlashAttention\\\\nhas better IO complexity than FlashAttention by a factor proportional to the sparsity ratio. We discuss\\\\nfurther extensions to other operations (attention on multi-GPU, kernel regression, block-sparse matrix\\\\n2\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 3 ---\\\\nmultiply) in Section 5. We open-source FlashAttention to make it easier to build on this primitive.1\\\\nWe empirically validate that FlashAttention speeds up model training and improves model quality by\\\\nmodeling longer context. We also benchmark the runtime and memory footprint of FlashAttention and\\\\nblock-sparse FlashAttention compared to prior attention implementations.\\\\n• Faster Model Training. FlashAttention trains Transformer models faster in wall-clock time. Up to sequence length of 512,\\\\nFlashAttention is both faster and more memory-eﬃcient than any existing attention method, whereas\\\\nfor sequence length beyond 1K, some approximate attention methods (e.g., Linformer) start to become\\\\nfaster. On the other hand, block-sparse FlashAttention is faster than all existing approximate attention\\\\nmethods that we know of.\\\\n2\\\\nBackground\\\\nWe provide some background on the performance characteristics of common deep learning operations on\\\\nmodern hardware (GPUs). We also describe the standard implementation of attention.\\\\n2.1\\\\nHardware Performance\\\\nWe focus here on GPUs. Performance on other hardware accelerators are similar [46, 48].\\\\nGPU Memory Hierarchy. The GPU memory hierarchy (Fig. 1 left) comprises multiple forms of\\\\nmemory of diﬀerent sizes and speeds, with smaller memory being faster. As an example, the A100 GPU\\\\nhas 40-80GB of high bandwidth memory (HBM) with bandwidth 1.5-2.0TB/s and 192KB of on-chip SRAM\\\\nper each of 108 streaming multiprocessors with bandwidth estimated around 19TB/s [44, 45]. The on-chip\\\\nSRAM is an order of magnitude faster than HBM but many orders of magnitude smaller in size. As compute\\\\nhas gotten faster relative to memory speed [61, 62, 63], operations are increasingly bottlenecked by memory\\\\n(HBM) accesses. Thus exploiting fast SRAM becomes more important.\\\\nExecution Model. GPUs have a massive number of threads to execute an operation (called a kernel).\\\\nEach kernel loads inputs from HBM to registers and SRAM, computes, then writes outputs to HBM.\\\\nPerformance characteristics. Depending on the balance of computation and memory accesses, op-\\\\nerations can be classiﬁed as either compute-bound or memory-bound. This is commonly measured by the\\\\narithmetic intensity [85], which is the number of arithmetic operations per byte of memory access.\\\\n1. Compute-bound: the time taken by the operation is determined by how many arithmetic operations there\\\\nare, while time accessing HBM is much smaller. Typical examples are matrix multiply with large inner\\\\ndimension, and convolution with large number of channels.\\\\n2. Memory-bound: the time taken by the operation is determined by the number of memory accesses, while\\\\ntime spent in computation is much smaller. Examples include most other operations: elementwise (e.g.,\\\\nactivation, dropout), and reduction (e.g., sum, softmax, batch norm, layer norm).\\\\nKernel fusion. The most common approach to accelerate memory-bound operations is kernel fusion: if\\\\nthere are multiple operations applied to the same input, the input can be loaded once from HBM, instead of\\\\nmultiple times for each operation. Compilers can automatically fuse many elementwise operations [53, 65, 75].\\\\n1FlashAttention code is available at https://github.com/HazyResearch/flash-attention\\\\n3\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 4 ---\\\\nHowever, in the context of model training, the intermediate values still need to be written to HBM to save\\\\nfor the backward pass, reducing the eﬀectiveness of naive kernel fusion.\\\\n2.2\\\\nStandard Attention Implementation\\\\nGiven input sequences Q, K, V ∈R𝑁×𝑑where 𝑁is the sequence length and 𝑑is the head dimension, we want\\\\nto compute the attention output O ∈R𝑁×𝑑:\\\\nS = QK⊤∈R𝑁×𝑁,\\\\nP = softmax(S) ∈R𝑁×𝑁,\\\\nO = PV ∈R𝑁×𝑑,\\\\nwhere softmax is applied row-wise.\\\\nStandard attention implementations materialize the matrices S and P to HBM, which takes 𝑂(𝑁2) memory.\\\\nOften 𝑁≫𝑑(e.g., for GPT2, 𝑁= 1024 and 𝑑= 64). We describe the standard attention implementation\\\\nin Algorithm 0. As some or most of the operations are memory-bound (e.g., softmax), the large number of\\\\nmemory accesses translates to slow wall-clock time.\\\\nThis problem is exacerbated by other elementwise operations applied to the attention matrix, such as\\\\nmasking applied to S or dropout applied to P. As a result, there have been many attempts to fuse several\\\\nelementwise operations, such as fusing masking with softmax [77].\\\\nIn Section 3.2, we will show that the standard attention implementation performs HBM accesses quadratic\\\\nin the sequence length 𝑁. We also compare the number of FLOPs and number of HBM accesses of standard\\\\nattention and of our method (FlashAttention).\\\\nAlgorithm 0 Standard Attention Implementation\\\\nRequire: Matrices Q, K, V ∈R𝑁×𝑑in HBM.\\\\n1: Load Q, K by blocks from HBM, compute S = QK⊤, write S to HBM.\\\\n2: Read S from HBM, compute P = softmax(S), write P to HBM.\\\\n3: Load P and V by blocks from HBM, compute O = PV, write O to HBM.\\\\n4: Return O.\\\\n3\\\\nFlashAttention: Algorithm, Analysis, and Extensions\\\\nWe show how to compute exact attention with fewer HBM reads/writes and without storing large intermediate\\\\nmatrices for the backward pass. This yields an attention algorithm that is both memory eﬃcient and faster in\\\\nwall-clock time. We analyze its IO complexity, showing that our method requires much fewer HBM accesses\\\\ncompared to standard attention. We further show that FlashAttention can serve as a useful primitive by\\\\nextending it to handle block-sparse attention.\\\\nWe focus here on the forward pass for ease of exposition; Appendix B contains details for the backward.\\\\n3.1\\\\nAn Eﬃcient Attention Algorithm With Tiling and Recomputation\\\\nGiven the inputs Q, K, V ∈R𝑁×𝑑in HBM, we aim to compute the attention output O ∈R𝑁×𝑑and write it to\\\\nHBM. Our goal is to reduce the amount of HBM accesses (to sub-quadratic in 𝑁).\\\\nWe apply two established techniques (tiling, recomputation) to overcome the technical challenge of\\\\ncomputing exact attention in sub-quadratic HBM accesses. We describe this in Algorithm 1. The main idea\\\\nis that we split the inputs Q, K, V into blocks, load them from slow HBM to fast SRAM, then compute the\\\\nattention output with respect to those blocks. By scaling the output of each block by the right normalization\\\\nfactor before adding them up, we get the correct result at the end.\\\\nTiling. We compute attention by blocks. Softmax couples columns of K, so we decompose the large\\\\nsoftmax with scaling [51, 60, 66].\\\\nFor numerical stability, the softmax of vector 𝑥∈R𝐵is computed as:\\\\n𝑚(𝑥) := max\\\\n𝑖\\\\n𝑥𝑖,\\\\n𝑓(𝑥) :=\\\\n\\\\u0002\\\\n𝑒𝑥1−𝑚(𝑥)\\\\n. . .\\\\n𝑒𝑥𝐵−𝑚(𝑥)\\\\u0003\\\\n,\\\\nℓ(𝑥) :=\\\\n∑︁\\\\n𝑖\\\\n𝑓(𝑥)𝑖,\\\\nsoftmax(𝑥) := 𝑓(𝑥)\\\\nℓ(𝑥) .\\\\n4\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 5 ---\\\\nFor vectors 𝑥(1), 𝑥(2) ∈R𝐵, we can decompose the softmax of the concatenated 𝑥=\\\\n\\\\u0002\\\\n𝑥(1) 𝑥(2)\\\\u0003\\\\n∈R2𝐵as:\\\\n𝑚(𝑥) = 𝑚(\\\\n\\\\u0002\\\\n𝑥(1) 𝑥(2)\\\\u0003\\\\n) = max(𝑚(𝑥(1)), 𝑚(𝑥(2))),\\\\n𝑓(𝑥) =\\\\nh\\\\n𝑒𝑚(𝑥(1))−𝑚(𝑥) 𝑓(𝑥(1))\\\\n𝑒𝑚(𝑥(2))−𝑚(𝑥) 𝑓(𝑥(2))\\\\ni\\\\n,\\\\nℓ(𝑥) = ℓ(\\\\n\\\\u0002\\\\n𝑥(1) 𝑥(2)\\\\u0003\\\\n) = 𝑒𝑚(𝑥(1))−𝑚(𝑥)ℓ(𝑥(1)) + 𝑒𝑚(𝑥(2))−𝑚(𝑥)ℓ(𝑥(2)),\\\\nsoftmax(𝑥) = 𝑓(𝑥)\\\\nℓ(𝑥) .\\\\nTherefore if we keep track of some extra statistics (𝑚(𝑥), ℓ(𝑥)), we can compute softmax one block at a time.2\\\\nWe thus split the inputs Q, K, V into blocks (Algorithm 1 line 3), compute the softmax values along with\\\\nextra statistics (Algorithm 1 line 10), and combine the results (Algorithm 1 line 12).\\\\nRecomputation. One of our goals is to not store 𝑂(𝑁2) intermediate values for the backward pass. The\\\\nbackward pass typically requires the matrices S, P ∈R𝑁×𝑁to compute the gradients with respect to Q, K, V.\\\\nHowever, by storing the output O and the softmax normalization statistics (𝑚, ℓ), we can recompute the\\\\nattention matrix S and P easily in the backward pass from blocks of Q, K, V in SRAM. This can be seen as a\\\\nform of selective gradient checkpointing [10, 34]. While gradient checkpointing has been suggested to reduce\\\\nthe maximum amount of memory required [66], all implementations (that we know oﬀ) have to trade speed\\\\nfor memory. In contrast, even with more FLOPs, our recomputation speeds up the backward pass due to\\\\nreduced HBM accesses (Fig. 2). The full backward pass description is in Appendix B.\\\\nImplementation details:\\\\nKernel fusion.\\\\nTiling enables us to implement our algorithm in one\\\\nCUDA kernel, loading input from HBM, performing all the computation steps (matrix multiply, softmax,\\\\noptionally masking and dropout, matrix multiply), then write the result back to HBM (masking and dropout\\\\nin Appendix B). This avoids repeatedly reading and writing of inputs and outputs from and to HBM.\\\\nAlgorithm 1 FlashAttention\\\\nRequire: Matrices Q, K, V ∈R𝑁×𝑑in HBM, on-chip SRAM of size 𝑀.\\\\n1: Set block sizes 𝐵𝑐=\\\\n\\\\u0006 𝑀\\\\n4𝑑\\\\n\\\\u0007\\\\n, 𝐵𝑟= min \\\\u0000\\\\u0006 𝑀\\\\n4𝑑\\\\n\\\\u0007\\\\n, 𝑑\\\\u0001.\\\\n2: Initialize O = (0)𝑁×𝑑∈R𝑁×𝑑, ℓ= (0)𝑁∈R𝑁, 𝑚= (−∞)𝑁∈R𝑁in HBM.\\\\n3: Divide Q into 𝑇𝑟=\\\\nl\\\\n𝑁\\\\n𝐵𝑟\\\\nm\\\\nblocks Q1, . . . , Q𝑇𝑟of size 𝐵𝑟× 𝑑each, and divide K, V in to 𝑇𝑐=\\\\nl\\\\n𝑁\\\\n𝐵𝑐\\\\nm\\\\nblocks\\\\nK1, . . . , K𝑇𝑐and V1, . . . , V𝑇𝑐, of size 𝐵𝑐× 𝑑each.\\\\n4: Divide O into 𝑇𝑟blocks O𝑖, . . . , O𝑇𝑟of size 𝐵𝑟× 𝑑each, divide ℓinto 𝑇𝑟blocks ℓ𝑖, . . . , ℓ𝑇𝑟of size 𝐵𝑟each,\\\\ndivide 𝑚into 𝑇𝑟blocks 𝑚1, . . . , 𝑚𝑇𝑟of size 𝐵𝑟each.\\\\n5: for 1 ≤𝑗≤𝑇𝑐do\\\\n6:\\\\nLoad K 𝑗, V𝑗from HBM to on-chip SRAM.\\\\n7:\\\\nfor 1 ≤𝑖≤𝑇𝑟do\\\\n8:\\\\nLoad Q𝑖, O𝑖, ℓ𝑖, 𝑚𝑖from HBM to on-chip SRAM.\\\\n9:\\\\nOn chip, compute S𝑖𝑗= Q𝑖K𝑇\\\\n𝑗∈R𝐵𝑟×𝐵𝑐.\\\\n10:\\\\nOn chip, compute ˜𝑚𝑖𝑗= rowmax(S𝑖𝑗) ∈R𝐵𝑟, ˜P𝑖𝑗= exp(S𝑖𝑗−˜𝑚𝑖𝑗) ∈R𝐵𝑟×𝐵𝑐(pointwise), ˜ℓ𝑖𝑗=\\\\nrowsum(˜P𝑖𝑗) ∈R𝐵𝑟.\\\\n11:\\\\nOn chip, compute 𝑚new\\\\n𝑖\\\\n= max(𝑚𝑖, ˜𝑚𝑖𝑗) ∈R𝐵𝑟, ℓnew\\\\n𝑖\\\\n= 𝑒𝑚𝑖−𝑚new\\\\n𝑖\\\\nℓ𝑖+ 𝑒˜𝑚𝑖𝑗−𝑚new\\\\n𝑖\\\\n˜ℓ𝑖𝑗∈R𝐵𝑟.\\\\n12:\\\\nWrite O𝑖←diag(ℓnew\\\\n𝑖\\\\n)−1(diag(ℓ𝑖)𝑒𝑚𝑖−𝑚new\\\\n𝑖\\\\nO𝑖+ 𝑒˜𝑚𝑖𝑗−𝑚new\\\\n𝑖\\\\n˜P𝑖𝑗V𝑗) to HBM.\\\\n13:\\\\nWrite ℓ𝑖←ℓnew\\\\n𝑖\\\\n, 𝑚𝑖←𝑚new\\\\n𝑖\\\\nto HBM.\\\\n14:\\\\nend for\\\\n15: end for\\\\n16: Return O.\\\\nWe show FlashAttention’s correctness, runtime, and memory requirement (proof in Appendix C).\\\\nTheorem 1. Algorithm 1 returns O = softmax(QK⊤)V with 𝑂(𝑁2𝑑) FLOPs and requires 𝑂(𝑁) additional\\\\nmemory beyond inputs and output.\\\\n3.2\\\\nAnalysis: IO Complexity of FlashAttention\\\\nWe analyze the IO complexity of FlashAttention, showing signiﬁcant reduction in HBM accesses compared\\\\nto standard attention. We also provide a lower bound, proving that no exact attention algorithm can\\\\n2This style of aggregation is called algebraic aggregation [33].\\\\n5\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 6 ---\\\\nAttention\\\\nStandard\\\\nFlashAttention\\\\nGFLOPs\\\\n66.6\\\\n75.2\\\\nHBM R/W (GB)\\\\n40.3\\\\n4.4\\\\nRuntime (ms)\\\\n41.7\\\\n7.3\\\\nSparsity Speedup\\\\n% Non-Zero Blocks\\\\n20\\\\n60\\\\n50\\\\n100\\\\n150\\\\nFwd + Bwd (ms)\\\\nEﬀect of Block Size\\\\nBlock Size\\\\n64 128\\\\n256\\\\n512\\\\nFwd Runtime (ms)\\\\n6\\\\n2\\\\nHBM Accesses (GB)\\\\nDense\\\\nFlashAttention\\\\nBlock-Sparse\\\\nFlashAttention\\\\n2\\\\n4\\\\n6\\\\nRuntime\\\\nHBM\\\\nAccesses\\\\nFigure 2:\\\\nLeft: Forward + backward runtime of standard attention and FlashAttention for GPT-2 medium\\\\n(seq. length 1024, head dim. 64, 16 heads, batch size 64) on A100 GPU. Proofs are in Appendix C.\\\\nTheorem 2. Let 𝑁be the sequence length, 𝑑be the head dimension, and 𝑀be size of SRAM with 𝑑≤𝑀≤𝑁𝑑.\\\\nStandard attention (Algorithm 0) requires Θ(𝑁𝑑+ 𝑁2) HBM accesses, while FlashAttention (Algorithm 1)\\\\nrequires Θ(𝑁2𝑑2𝑀−1) HBM accesses.\\\\nFor typical values of 𝑑(64-128) and 𝑀(around 100KB), 𝑑2 is many times smaller than 𝑀, and thus\\\\nFlashAttention requires many times fewer HBM accesses than standard implementation. This leads to\\\\nboth faster execution and lower memory footprint, which we validate in Section 4.3.\\\\nThe main idea of the proof is that given the SRAM size of 𝑀, we can load blocks of K, V of size Θ(𝑀) each\\\\n(Algorithm 1 line 6). For each block of K and V, we iterate over all blocks of Q (Algorithm 1 line 8) to compute\\\\nthe intermediate values, resulting in Θ(𝑁𝑑𝑀−1) passes over Q. Each pass loads Θ(𝑁𝑑) elements, which\\\\namounts to Θ(𝑁2𝑑2𝑀−1) HBM accesses. We similarly prove that the backward pass of standard attention\\\\nrequires Θ(𝑁𝑑+ 𝑁2) HBM accesses while the backward pass of FlashAttention requires Θ(𝑁2𝑑2𝑀−1)\\\\nHBM accesses (Appendix B).\\\\nWe prove a lower-bound: one cannot asymptotically improve on the number of HBM accesses for all\\\\nvalues of 𝑀(the SRAM size) when computing exact attention.\\\\nProposition 3. Let 𝑁be the sequence length, 𝑑be the head dimension, and 𝑀be size of SRAM with\\\\n𝑑≤𝑀≤𝑁𝑑. There does not exist an algorithm to compute exact attention with 𝑜(𝑁2𝑑2𝑀−1) HBM accesses\\\\nfor all 𝑀in the range [𝑑, 𝑁𝑑].\\\\nThe proof relies on the fact that for 𝑀= Θ(𝑁𝑑) any algorithm must perform Ω(𝑁2𝑑2𝑀−1) = Ω(𝑁𝑑)\\\\nHBM accesses. This type of lower bound over a subrange of 𝑀is common in the streaming algorithms\\\\nliterature [88]. We leave proving parameterized complexity [27] lower bounds in terms of 𝑀as exciting future\\\\nwork.\\\\nWe validate that the number of HBM accesses is the main determining factor of attention run-time.\\\\nIn Fig. 2 (left), we see that even though FlashAttention has higher FLOP count compared to standard\\\\nattention (due to recomputation in the backward pass), it has much fewer HBM accesses, resulting in much\\\\nfaster runtime. In Fig. 2 (middle), we vary the block size 𝐵𝑐of FlashAttention, which results in diﬀerent\\\\namounts of HBM accesses, and measure the runtime of the forward pass. As block size increases, the number\\\\nof HBM accesses decreases (as we make fewer passes over the input), and runtime decreases. For large enough\\\\nblock size (beyond 256), the runtime is then bottlenecked by other factors (e.g., arithmetic operations).\\\\nMoreover, larger block size will not ﬁt into the small SRAM size.\\\\n3.3\\\\nExtension: Block-Sparse FlashAttention\\\\nWe extend FlashAttention to approximate attention: we propose block-sparse FlashAttention, whose\\\\nIO complexity is smaller than FlashAttention by a factor proportional to the sparsity.\\\\nGiven inputs Q, K, V ∈R𝑁×𝑑and a mask matrix ˜M ∈{0, 1}𝑁×𝑁, we want to compute:\\\\nS = QK⊤∈R𝑁×𝑁,\\\\nP = softmax(S ⊙𝟙˜M) ∈R𝑁×𝑁,\\\\nO = PV ∈R𝑁×𝑑,\\\\nwhere (S ⊙𝟙˜M)𝑘𝑙= S𝑘𝑙if ˜M𝑘𝑙= 1 and −∞if M𝑘𝑙= 0. We require ˜M to have block form: for some block sizes\\\\n𝐵𝑟, 𝐵𝑐, for all 𝑘, 𝑙, ˜M𝑘,𝑙= M𝑖𝑗with 𝑖= ⌊𝑘/𝐵𝑟⌋, 𝑗= ⌊𝑙/𝐵𝑐⌋for some M ∈{0, 1}𝑁/𝐵𝑟×𝑁/𝐵𝑐.\\\\n6\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 7 ---\\\\nGiven a predeﬁned block sparsity mask M ∈{0, 1}𝑁/𝐵𝑟×𝑁/𝐵𝑐we can easily adapt Algorithm 1 to only\\\\ncompute the nonzero blocks of the attention matrix. The algorithm is identical to Algorithm 1, except we\\\\nskip zero blocks. We reproduce the algorithm description in Algorithm 5 in Appendix B.\\\\nWe also analyze the IO complexity of block-sparse FlashAttention.\\\\nProposition 4. Let 𝑁be the sequence length, 𝑑be the head dimension, and 𝑀be size of SRAM with\\\\n𝑑≤𝑀≤𝑁𝑑. Block-sparse FlashAttention (Algorithm 5) requires Θ(𝑁𝑑+ 𝑁2𝑑2𝑀−1𝑠) HBM accesses\\\\nwhere 𝑠is the fraction of nonzero blocks in the block-sparsity mask.\\\\nWe see that applying block-sparsity yields a direct improvement by the sparsity to the larger term in the\\\\nIO complexity. For large sequence lengths 𝑁, 𝑠is often set to 𝑁−1/2 [11] or 𝑁−1 log 𝑁[3, 17, 92], resulting\\\\nin Θ(𝑁\\\\n√\\\\n𝑁) or Θ(𝑁log 𝑁) IO complexity. For downstream experiments, we use the ﬁxed butterﬂy sparsity\\\\npattern [17], which has been shown to be able to approximate arbitrary sparsity [16].\\\\nIn Fig. 2 (right), we validate that as the sparsity increases, the runtime of block-sparse FlashAttention\\\\nimproves proportionally. On the LRA benchmark, block-sparse FlashAttention achieves 2.8× speedup,\\\\nwhile performing on par with standard attention (Section 4).\\\\n4\\\\nExperiments\\\\nWe evaluate the impact of using FlashAttention to train Transformer models. We validate two claims\\\\nabout training time and model accuracy, and report attention runtime and memory benchmarks.\\\\n• Training Speed. FlashAttention outperforms the MLPerf 1.1 [58] speed record for BERT by 15%, and\\\\nspeeds up GPT-2 up to 3× over HuggingFace [87] and 1.8× over Megatron [77] over standard Transformers.\\\\nFlashAttention speeds up the long-range arena (LRA) benchmark 2.4×.\\\\n• Quality. FlashAttention scales Transformers to longer sequences, yielding higher quality. FlashAt-\\\\ntention trains GPT-2 with context length 4K faster than Megatron trains GPT-2 with context length\\\\n1K, while achieving 0.7 better perplexity. Modeling longer sequences yields 6.4 points of lift on two long-\\\\ndocument classiﬁcation tasks. Finally, FlashAttention yields the ﬁrst Transformer that can achieve\\\\nbetter-than-random performance on the challenging Path-X task (sequence length 16K), and block-sparse\\\\nFlashAttention yields the ﬁrst sequence model that we know of that can achieve better-than-random\\\\nperformance on Path-256 (sequence length 64K).\\\\n• Benchmarking Attention. We measure the runtime and memory performance of FlashAttention\\\\nand block-sparse FlashAttention based on sequence length. We conﬁrm that the memory footprint\\\\nof FlashAttention scales linearly with seq. length and is up to 3× faster than standard attention for\\\\ncommon seq. lengths (up to 2K). We conﬁrm that runtime of block-sparse FlashAttention scales linearly\\\\nin seq. length and is faster than all existing approximate attention baselines.\\\\nAdditional experiment details are in Appendix E.\\\\n4.1\\\\nFaster Models with FlashAttention\\\\nBERT.\\\\nFlashAttention yields the fastest single-node BERT training speed that we know of. FlashAttention\\\\nand block-sparse FlashAttention have the same memory footprint, which grows linearly with sequence\\\\nlength. FlashAttention is up to 20× more memory eﬃcient than exact attention baselines, and is more\\\\nmemory-eﬃcient than the approximate attention baselines. All other algorithms except for Linformer run\\\\nout of memory on an A100 GPU before 64K, and FlashAttention is still 2× more eﬃcient than Linformer.\\\\n5\\\\nLimitations and Future Directions\\\\nWe discuss limitations of our approach and future directions. Related work is given in Appendix A.\\\\nCompiling to CUDA. Our current approach to building IO-aware implementations of attention requires\\\\nwriting a new CUDA kernel for each new attention implementation. This requires writing the attention\\\\nalgorithm in a considerably lower-level language than PyTorch, and requires signiﬁcant engineering eﬀort.\\\\nImplementations may also not be transferrable across GPU architectures. These limitations suggest the\\\\nneed for a method that supports writing attention algorithms in a high-level language (e.g., PyTorch), and\\\\ncompiling to IO-aware implementations in CUDA—similar to eﬀorts such as Halide in image processing [70].\\\\nIO-Aware Deep Learning. We believe that the IO-aware approach can extend beyond attention.\\\\nAttention is the most memory-intensive computation in Transformers, but every layer in a deep network\\\\ntouches GPU HBM. We hope our work inspires IO-aware implementations of additional modules. We discuss\\\\nthese potential extensions in Appendix D.\\\\nMulti-GPU IO-Aware Methods. Our IO-aware implementation of attention is optimal within con-\\\\nstants for computing attention on a single GPU. However, the attention computation may be parallelizable\\\\nacross multiple GPUs [72]. Using multiple GPUs adds an additional layer to IO analysis—accounting for\\\\ndata transfer between GPUs. We hope our work inspires future work in this direction.\\\\nAcknowledgments\\\\nOur implementation uses Apex’s FMHA code (https://github.com/NVIDIA/apex/tree/master/apex/\\\\ncontrib/csrc/fmha) as a starting point. Long-short transformer: Eﬃcient transformers for language and vision. Advances in\\\\nNeural Information Processing Systems, 34, 2021.\\\\n16\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 17 ---\\\\nA\\\\nRelated Work\\\\nIO-Aware Runtime Optimization. The broad concept of optimizing for reading and writing to fast/slow\\\\nmemory has a long history in computer science and has been known by many names. We draw the most\\\\ndirect connection to the literature of analyzing I/O complexity in this work [1], but concepts of memory\\\\nhierarchies are fundamental and has appeared in many forms, from the working set model [21], to data\\\\nlocality [86], to the Rooﬂine model of arithmetic intensity [85], to analyses of scalability [59], to standard\\\\ntextbook treatments of computer architecture [40]. We hope that this work encourages the community to\\\\nadopt these ideas in more parts of the deep learning stack.\\\\nEﬃcient ML Models with Structured Matrices. Matrix multiply is the core computational bottle-\\\\nneck of most machine learning models. To reduce the computational complexity, there have been numerous\\\\napproaches to learn over a more eﬃcient set of matrices. These matrices are called structured matrices, which\\\\nhave subquadratic (𝑜(𝑛2) for dimension 𝑛× 𝑛) number of parameters and runtime. Most common examples\\\\nof structured matrices are sparse and low-rank matrices, along with fast transforms commonly encountered\\\\nin signal processing (Fourier, Chebyshev, sine/cosine, orthogonal polynomials). There have been several\\\\nmore general classes of structured matrices proposed in machine learning: Toeplitz-like [78], low-displacement\\\\nrank [49], quasi-separable [25]). The butterﬂy pattern we use for our block-sparse attention is motivated\\\\nby the fact that butterﬂy matrices [15, 64] and their products have been shown to be able to express any\\\\nstructured matrices with almost optimal runtime and number of parameters [16, 20]. However, even though\\\\nstructured matrices are eﬃcient in theory, they have not seen wide adoption since it is hard to translate their\\\\neﬃciency to wall-clock speedup since dense unconstrained matrix multiply has very optimize implementation,\\\\na phenomenon known as the hardware lottery [41]. Extensions of butterﬂy matrices [17, 18] aimed to make\\\\nbutterﬂy matrices more hardware-friendly.\\\\nSparse Training. Our block-sparse FlashAttention can be seen as a step towards making sparse model\\\\ntraining more eﬃcient. Sparse models have seen success in compressing models for inference (pruning) by\\\\nsparsifying the weight matrices [23, 38, 39, 55, 76]. For model training, the lottery tickets hypothesis [28, 29, 30]\\\\nsuggests that there are a set of small sub-networks derived from a larger dense network that performs as\\\\nwell as the original dense network. Out block-sparse FlashAttention can also be seen as a ﬁxed lottery\\\\nticket in the context of attention: we ﬁx the sparsity pattern to be the butterﬂy pattern through training,\\\\nand observe that it performs almost as well as the (dense) FlashAttention on the Long-range Arena tasks.\\\\nEﬃcient Transformer. Transformer-based models have become the most widely-used architecture in\\\\nnatural language processing [22] and computer vision [24, 91]. However, one of their computational bottlenecks\\\\nis that their time and memory scales quadratic in the sequence length. There are numerous approaches to\\\\novercome this bottleneck, including approximation with hashing (i.e., sparse) such as Reformer [51] and\\\\nSmyrf [19] and with low-rank approximation such as Performer [12, 54]. One can even combine sparse and\\\\nlow-rank approximation for better accuracy (e.g., Longformer [3], BigBird [92], Scatterbrain [9], Long-short\\\\ntransformer [94], Combiner [73]). Other approaches include compressing along the sequence dimension to\\\\nattend to multiple tokens at once [52, 57, 79, 89]. One can also attend over the states from previous sequences\\\\nto help lengthen the context (e.g., Transformer-XL [14] and Compressive Transformer [69]). We recommend\\\\nthe survey [81] for more details.\\\\nThere are several lines of work on developing other modules instead of attention to model longer context.\\\\nHiPPO [35] and its extensions, most notably S4 [31, 36, 37] projects the history on a polynomial basis,\\\\nallowing accurate reconstruction of the history through state-space models. They combine the strengths of\\\\nCNNs (eﬃcient training), RNNs (eﬃcient inference), and continuous models (robust to change in sampling\\\\nrates). LambdaNetworks [2], AFT [93] and FLASH [42] are other attempts at replacing attention in the\\\\ncontext of image classiﬁcation and language modeling.\\\\nB\\\\nAlgorithm Details\\\\nWe ﬁrst derive the forward and backward passes of attention and show that they can be computed in a\\\\nmemory-eﬃcient manner (requiring extra memory linear instead of quadratic in the sequence length). Though\\\\nthey reduce the amount of extra memory required, naively they still incur quadratic HBM accesses, resulting\\\\nin slower execution speed. We describe the FlashAttention algorithm to implement both the forward\\\\n17\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 18 ---\\\\nand the backward passes on GPUs that reduces HBM accesses, leading to both faster runtime and smaller\\\\nmemory footprint.\\\\nB.1\\\\nMemory-eﬃcient forward pass\\\\nThe main challenge in making attention memory-eﬃcient is the softmax that couples the columns of K (and\\\\ncolumns of V). Our approach is to compute the softmax normalization constant separately to decouple the\\\\ncolumns. This technique [60] has been used in the literature [51, 66] to show that attention computation\\\\ndoes not need quadratic extra memory (though the number of HBM accesses is still quadratic, resulting in\\\\nslow run-time).\\\\nFor simplicity, we omit here the max-shifting step during softmax.
